‒ this document concerns the conclusion of the agreement on scientific and technological cooperation between the european union and the faroe islands. on 18 march 2014, the council authorised the european commission to open negotiations, on behalf of the european union, with the faroe islands for an agreement to associate the faroe islands to horizon 2020 - the framework programme for research and innovation (2014-2020). the faroe islands should participate as an associated country under the terms and conditions set out in horizon 2020 and in council decision 2013/743/eu. the cooperation agreement will include regular discussions on cooperation and development prospects, regular information on the implementation of research programmes and projects, meetings and visits with exchange of views between researchers and technicians, participation of experts in seminars, symposia and workshops. an eu-faroe research and innovation committee should be set up, which should be composed of representatives of both parties. we voted yes.
‒ the report proposes to improve the functioning of eu financial markets by applying rules that seek to minimise the effects of identified inefficiencies, which are mainly linked to insufficient shareholder involvement and a lack of an adequate level of transparency. the following objectives are advocated, among others: to increase the involvement of owners and asset managers in their respective joint-stock companies; to create a better link between the remuneration and performance of company directors; to increase transparency and shareholder oversight of related party transactions; to encourage a more long-term oriented perspective. we voted in favour of all the amendments calling for more transparency, shareholder identification, better information and the possibility for workers' representatives to have a vote on the remuneration policy of directors. however, the report's approach is frankly reductive. without downplaying the problem of diminished shareholder involvement or lack of adequate levels of transparency, the underlying issue is another and concerns the essence of globalised capitalism, the free movement of capital and the growing inequalities in the distribution of income. some of these aspects are simply ignored by the report. any gains from the application of the guidelines now adopted will not serve to ensure a fairer redistribution of the wealth created.
‒ this report enhances transparency by creating country-by-country reports, which require companies to provide a list of all shareholders with more than 0.5% of the company's outstanding shares, or by encouraging companies to publish the minutes of their general meetings and the results of votes on their websites, which is an important step in the fight against tax havens and tax evasion. it also includes the need to justify the bonuses paid. all these are important measures to combat tax evasion and tax havens. so i voted in favour.
‒ the overall objective of this proposal for a revision of the shareholder rights directive is to contribute to the long-term sustainability of eu companies, to create an attractive environment for shareholders and to increase the exercise of cross-border voting rights by increasing the efficiency of the equity investment chain in order to contribute to growth, job creation and competitiveness in the eu. the proposal also responds to the commitment made in the context of a renewed strategy for long-term financing of the european economy. it contributes to a more long-term shareholder perspective, which ensures better operating conditions for listed companies. that is why i am voting in favour.
‒ directive 2007/36/ec of the european parliament and of the council lays down requirements for the exercise of certain shareholder rights attaching to shares with the right to vote at general meetings of companies which have their registered office in a member state and whose shares are admitted to trading on a regulated market situated or operating in a member state. i agree that although shareholders do not own the companies, which are separate legal entities outside their full control, they do have a relevant role in the governance of these companies. i am voting in favour of this proposal for a directive because i believe that greater shareholder participation in the governance of companies is one of the instruments which can contribute to improving both the financial and non-financial performance of companies. however, and given that shareholder rights are not the only factor that can contribute to a long-term approach to corporate governance, i believe that this factor should be accompanied by additional measures to ensure greater involvement of the different actors involved, in particular workers, local authorities and civil society.
‒ this report requires large companies and public interest entities to disclose country-by-country information on profits earned, taxes paid and subsidies received. i voted in favour of this report because this proposal for a revision aims to ensure greater involvement of shareholders in the companies in which they invest and thus contribute to their long-term competitiveness and sustainability. the rules on shareholder identification, the transmission of information, reporting obligations and employee involvement are also strengthened. in addition, portugal is one of the 15 eu member states that already requires disclosure of directors' remuneration policy hence my affirmative vote . i 'm not .
‒ after luxleaks and similar cases, this report represents a good opportunity to introduce transparency in large companies and economic groups and thus combat tax evasion and fraud. in addition to greater shareholder involvement in business life, with a say in, for example, remuneration policy, the report also requires large companies and public interest entities to disclose country-by-country information on profits earned, taxes paid and subsidies received. this clarifies for citizens and competent authorities whether companies pay the taxes due where they actually carry out their economic activities.
in writing. ‒ directive 2007/36/ec of the european parliament and of the council lays down requirements for the exercise of certain shareholder rights attached to shares with voting rights at general meetings of companies which have their registered office in a member state and whose shares are admitted to trading on a regulated market situated or operating in a member state. although they are not the 'owners' of companies, shareholders play a significant role in the governance of these companies. however, the financial crisis has revealed that in many cases shareholders have supported excessive short-term risk-taking by managers. for this reason, greater shareholder participation in corporate governance is one of the instruments that can contribute to improving both the financial and non-financial performance of companies and that is why i support this proposal to revise directive 2007/36/ec on the exercise of certain rights of shareholders in listed companies, as i believe that this also contributes to their long-term sustainability.
‒ large companies should conduct their tax affairs in a manner consistent with the service they receive from their employees and society. there is a disproportion between the ability of a large firm to finance itself and adapt to adverse market conditions and that of an individual in the same circumstances. it is up to the public authorities to correct this disproportion by moralizing the behaviour of large companies, which are not amorphous entities after all: they are made up of individuals and for individuals. private enterprise should be promoted and rewarded, but in proportion to the creation of jobs and added value for the society in which it is embedded, and this principle should be enshrined in the relevant regulations.
‒ this directive aims to ensure better involvement of shareholders in company decisions. it identifies a certain short-sightedness on the part of company management that is too focused on short-term profitability, even calling into question the long-term sustainability of companies. however, this directive is paradoxical because it ignores or pretends to ignore that it is precisely the shareholders who want short-term profits, as is moreover completely identified in the subject of the conflict between the principal and the agent. in this sense, in addition to not ensuring shareholder involvement insofar as shareholders are completely sprayed through investment funds, this directive puts the question in reverse. the key to aligning company decisions with long-term sustainable management is to involve local workers and agents in the strategic decisions of companies. the directive puts the problem of wage differentials within the company, but again, it does not propose anything substantial to solve the problem.
in writing. ‒ the report under review relates to the amendment of directives 2007/36/ec and 2013/34/eu and proposes to improve the functioning of eu financial markets by identifying the following objectives: to increase the level and quality of the involvement of owners and asset managers in their investee companies; to create a better link between the remuneration and performance of company directors; to increase transparency and shareholder oversight of related party transactions; to ensure the reliability and quality of advisors' voting opinions; to simplify the transmission of information across the investment chain. we voted in favour of all the amendments calling for more transparency, shareholder identification, better information, and the possibility of giving workers' representatives the right to vote on the remuneration policy of directors. we believe that the problems in the financial sector are not due to a lack of shareholder involvement or an inadequate level of transparency. they are the fruit of the essence and logic of capitalism, the pursuit of higher profits. on the other hand, any gains which may result from the application of the rules now adopted will not serve to redistribute the wealth created more fairly but rather to increase the fortunes of the lords of money. we voted against it.
‒ the reform of the eu emissions trading system (eu ets) aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and combat climate change by addressing the imbalance between supply and demand for emission allowances, which undermines incentives to invest in green innovation. the estimated 2000 million surplus of allowances undermines the long-term cost-effectiveness of the scheme, making the ets not work as originally intended, and the commission has proposed (and rightly so) a market stabilisation reserve which introduces rules in the ests directive to govern market fluctuations and the supply of allowances. the commission should be able to assess the impact of the proposed measures on the environment and the climate change impact of the proposed measures. i therefore support the belet report, which reflects the commitment reached with member states after three trilogues, providing that if the surplus reaches a certain value, licences are withdrawn from the market and placed in a reserve to avoid imbalances, promoting the need for operators to invest in reducing co2 emissions, a mechanism to start as early as 2019, instead of the proposed date of 2021.
‒ this proposal is yet another demonstration of the outright and blatant failure of the greenhouse gas emission trading scheme (ghg) to achieve its stated objectives. since its creation in 2005, it has failed to reduce ghg emissions or drive any energy paradigm transition, but on the contrary, it has proven to be ineffective and perverse. it was clear during the debate that the supporters of the carbon market - the same ones who, having seen its failure, now want to make some amendments to it - have no answers to simple questions, such as the lack of examples of structural changes, significant from an environmental point of view, achieved through market instruments such as emissions trading. this is why it is time to move from a market-based approach to a regulatory approach that is economically and socially fair and environmentally effective, rather than patching up old wounds. what is born crooked, is later or never straightened. there will be those who will gain from this path. it's not the environment. let us recall, for example, the enormous permeability to fraud already demonstrated by the rcle (the thyssenkrupp and salzgitter cases, among others) and the fabulous profits achieved by some of the biggest polluters.
in writing. ‒ the european council conclusions of 23 and 24 october 2014 on a 2030 framework for climate and energy action state that an operational and reformed emissions trading scheme (ets), with a market stabilisation instrument, will be the main european instrument to achieve the union's greenhouse gas emission reduction target. that is why i am voting in favour.
‒ the commission presented a proposal for a market stabilisation reserve on 22 january 2014, together with a communication on a 2030 framework for climate and energy action. i would stress that the aim of the commission proposal is to make structural changes to the emissions trading system (ets) in order to address the issue of the surplus of allowances, currently estimated at 2 billion (which have been increasing in the system since 2009 (during phase 2)), and to rectify its shortcomings, in order to achieve its objective of 'promoting the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions under cost-effective and economically efficient conditions' (article 1 of the ets directive). although the 2020 greenhouse gas emissions target is guaranteed by the global emission limit, i would remind you that the surplus of allowances is undermining the cost-effectiveness of the scheme in the long term. the surplus is thus undermining the proper functioning of the carbon market and fundamentally the carbon price, thereby reducing the incentive to invest in low-carbon technologies.
in the first place, the commission has to be able to take account of the fact that the market is not yet in balance. the market stabilisation reserve (mrs) is an efficient tool that will stabilise our emissions trading scheme (ets) and thus save the central pillar of europe's sustainability and climate policy. the market stabilisation reserve is a crucial element in helping to ensure that carbon pricing stimulates innovation in energy efficiency. this reform puts europe on track to meet its 40% greenhouse gas emission reduction target by 2030 and also sends a strong signal to the climate negotiations to take place in december at cop21 in paris.
‒ the european commission has put forward a legislative proposal to revise the eu emissions trading system (ets), in line with the 2030 climate and energy framework agreed by eu leaders last october. the proposal aims at a more resilient and forward-looking energy union and climate policy which is, moreover, one of the priorities of the juncker commission. as part of the contribution to the new global climate agreement, which is due to be adopted in december, this is undeniably the first step towards the goal of reducing domestic greenhouse gas emissions by at least 40% by 2030. it is also intended to establish a market stabilisation reserve for the eu emissions trading system (eu ets) as part of the 2030 framework for climate and energy policies, given the current imbalance between supply and demand for emission allowances. we will thus be strengthening the functioning of the internal energy market at european level and ensuring that it operates in an economically efficient way, which is why i voted in favour of this legislative resolution.
‒ since its creation in 2005, the greenhouse gas emission trading scheme (ghges) has failed to reduce emissions in european countries, and there has been no real change in the way energy is produced and spent by industry. the ets is not an incentive to promote investment in clean energy solutions. on the contrary, it closes the door to really effective climate policies by discouraging regulations that are seen as interfering with the carbon price. given the massive number of permits available to pollute, the market has concluded that continuing to pollute is the cheapest option. so there is no investment in clean technologies or low carbon solutions, because there is a carbon market, which is designed to be attractive to industry, and trying to reform this system and equip it with instruments to stabilize it is just a cosmetic, lucrative operation to keep it looking attractive.
in writing. ‒ this proposal is yet another demonstration of the outright and blatant failure of the greenhouse gas emissions trading scheme (ghg ets), which since its inception in 2005 has failed to reduce ghg emissions or drive any energy paradigm transition. it was clear during the debate that the supporters of the carbon market - the same ones who, having seen its failure, now want to make some amendments to it - have no answers to simple questions, such as the lack of examples of structural changes, significant from an environmental point of view, achieved through market instruments such as emissions trading. this is why it is time to move from a market-based approach to a regulatory approach that is economically and socially fair and environmentally effective, rather than patching up old wounds.
‒ the report aims to remove the exclusion of seafarers from eu labour law. there is nothing in this particular report which contradicts our positions in defence of workers' rights. the changes brought about are therefore positive for these workers, which is why we voted in favour.
‒ i have tabled my vote in favour of the european parliament's draft legislative resolution on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on seafarers, amending a number of legislative texts. i welcome the commission proposal of 19 november 2013 for a directive aimed at improving the rights of seafarers by amending five directives on workers' rights to include seafarers in their scope.
‒ i support the european commission's proposal to improve the working conditions of seafarers on board ships flying the flag of one of the 28 member states of the european union, while taking into account the specificities of this sector of activity. the proposal for a directive thus corresponds to the revision of five previously adopted directives which provided for the exclusion of seafarers from their scope. the european commission recalled that the exclusions for seafarers in the five directives were not included in the commission's initial proposals and had been agreed before the negotiations with the other partners. i am voting in favour of the proposal because i believe that improving the working conditions of seafarers will help to give a new impetus to this sector and i believe that this will help to achieve the objective set by the european commission's blue book published on 10 october 2007, which set as its objective an increase in the number of workers in the maritime and fisheries sector and a qualitative increase in their working conditions, the first objective being impossible to achieve without the second.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report which aims to improve the working conditions of seafarers on board ships flying the flag of one of the 28 eu member states, while taking account of the specificities of this sector of activity. such improvement will contribute to achieving the objective set by the ec blue book (2007) which set as a target a qualitative increase in working conditions in the maritime sector, achieving better protection of workers and protecting competitiveness in the maritime transport sector which represents a challenge for the future of the eu.
‒ the purpose of this legislative resolution is to amend several european directives in order to improve the level of information and consultation of workers in the maritime sector. eu directives on labour law are generally applicable to all sectors of activity and to all categories of workers. however, seafarers are excluded or may be excluded from the scope of some directives, and there is no express justification for this situation. as a result, this proposal provides for the inclusion of seafarers in the scope of the employer's insolvency directive, the directive on collective redundancies and the directive on transfers of undertakings, and for specific provisions, in particular on information and consultation of workers and protection of their rights. the proposal for a directive on seafarers is also in line with the europe 2020 strategy and its employment objectives, respects fundamental rights and observes the principles recognised in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, which is why it deserved my vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ in the region where i come from, the autonomous region of the azores, everyone knows and recognises the special demands of the seafarer's profession, whether they are fishermen or workers in maritime transport. i therefore see in this legislative initiative of the european commission an opportunity to dignify and, essentially, to improve the working conditions of those who have to face the sea. i agree with the proposal in general terms and with some of the amendments proposed by the european parliament, in particular those which speed up the implementation of the directive in the member states, promote safety, improve working conditions by implementing new technological tools and promote ground-to-ship and vice versa communication. finally, i would stress the importance of collecting data on seafarers' activity, which will enable us to identify further possibilities for improvement. very important and consequential steps have already been taken with regard to fishing activity, but this approach needs to be extended to all activities at sea.

in writing. ‒ in july 2014, the commission presented a communication entitled 'towards a circular economy: an agenda to end waste in europe' aimed at designing and innovating for a circular economy, creating a policy framework to support resource efficiency and defining a specific strategic framework to enable smes to turn environmental challenges into environmentally sustainable business opportunities. moving towards a more circular economy is essential to delivering on the europe 2020 strategy on resource efficiency, promoting smart, sustainable and inclusive growth. this system will create added value for products and eliminate waste. in this respect, i agree with the rapporteur's position on the need to adopt legislative measures on waste by the end of 2015, proposing ambitious resource efficiency targets and reliable indicators. as regards the targets, one word to say that the principle of subsidiarity must always be safeguarded when setting binding targets for the member states with a view to resource efficiency, since the specificities inherent in each country cannot fail to be taken into account.
‒ i welcome this report with optimism. strengthening the circular economy in europe is a contribution to improving the global environment. every year, as a consequence of the still-prevailing linear economy, huge amounts of waste enter the seas, degrade and turn into even more dangerous pollutants, including so-called microplastics. on the other hand, high concentrations of carbon in the atmosphere acidify the oceans to levels that destroy the efficiency of ecosystems. the strategies set out in this report are imperative for global food security. the circular economy must be a winning strategy in europe and this model must be exported to the world.
‒ the legislative proposal on waste was controversially withdrawn by the commission a couple of months later and was strongly criticised by the european parliament, eu environment ministers and civil society. the report calls for significant improvements compared to the withdrawn commission proposal, as the commission did not make any proposal on binding reduction targets, calling for mandatory targets for the reduction of waste production by 2025. the commission is urged to present a new, more ambitious proposal by the end of 2015 reflecting waste prevention measures, binding waste reduction targets for municipal, industrial and commercial waste to be achieved by 2025, and calls for the application of the 'pay as you throw' principle for waste disposal to be combined with mandatory separate collection systems for paper, metal, plastic and glass, introducing the mandatory separate collection of biobased waste by 2020.
‒ i voted in favour of the pietikäinen report on resource efficiency: transition to a circular economy because i believe that the commitment to a circular economy, which allows for wealth creation by incorporating waste management into the value chain, is a smart and urgent commitment to the environmental, economic and social challenges that societies are facing at the same time. unregulated globalization leads to increased inequalities and our environmental footprint. the circular economy is an integrated and holistic approach to the challenges of globalisation, combining economic competitiveness and environmental sustainability, and enabling economic growth for current generations without compromising the development of future generations. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the union's policy on climate change and its impact on the environment.

in writing. ‒ we agree that legislation needs to be more appropriate and updated so that in the event of nuclear accidents, such as those at chernobyl and fukushima, swift and effective measures are taken to protect and ensure food safety for european consumers. the levels and guarantees proposed in the report for food safety were not sufficient. the 2013 revised codex alimentarius proposes specific criteria for radionuclides in food, points to more restrictive criteria, and the need for an emergency change in the established levels. the levels proposed in this report fall short of what is needed to protect consumers and the safety of europe's population in the event of a nuclear accident. codex also proposes the inclusion of other radioactive isotopes which have not been included in annex i.

in writing. ‒ in april 2010, the european commission put forward a proposal to recast regulation (euratom) no 3954/87 introducing maximum levels of contamination of food and feed following a nuclear accident or any other case of radiological emergency. i am in favour of this regulation setting maximum permitted levels of radioactive contamination of minor foodstuffs following a nuclear accident or any other case of radiological emergency and also maximum permitted levels of radioactive contamination of feedingstuffs following a nuclear accident or any other case of radiological emergency. the legal basis of this proposal required only a consultation of the european parliament. i support the new proposal which is the subject of this report, introducing some new elements which establish a clearer link with european food safety regulations.
‒ in the event of a radioactive accident or emergency, it is important that the european union has up-to-date legal instruments with simplified decision-making processes adapted to each situation to deal with situations such as those that occurred in the chernobyl and fukushima accidents. this council proposal, which is the subject of this report, introduces some new elements which establish a clearer link with european food safety regulations. i voted in favour of this report because food safety is the ultimate objective of the proposal.
‒ the council proposal for a regulation lays down maximum permitted levels of radioactive contamination of food and feed which may be placed on the european market following an accident or any other case of radiological emergency. it also lays down the procedures and implementing powers to make the pre-established maximum levels applicable. the proposal replaces regulation no 3954/87, which was established in 1987 following the chernobyl disaster, although the maximum permissible levels have not been changed. the maximum permitted levels apply to feed and food originating in the eu or imported from third countries, according to the place and circumstances of the nuclear accident or emergency. the report therefore calls for a change in the legal basis of the regulation for the articles on public health and the internal market in the lisbon treaty, reinforcing the implementing measures adopted in the event of a nuclear accident or other radiological emergency and updating the annexes to the regulation setting out the maximum permitted levels and the list of foods. i voted in favour of the report because i agree with the suggestions made by the rapporteur.
in writing. ‒ in april 2010, the european commission put forward a proposal to recast regulation (euratom) no 3954/87 introducing maximum levels of contamination of food and feed following a nuclear accident. the legal basis of this proposal required only a consultation of the european parliament. however, during the submission of this proposal, it was found that the provisions of regulation (euratom) no 3954/87 were not compatible with the new rules on 'comitology' introduced after the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon. the european commission has therefore decided to withdraw this draft and to submit a new one. the new proposal, which is the subject of this report, introduces some new elements which establish a clearer link with european food safety regulations. the proposal sets out in its annexes the maximum levels tolerated in the event of a radioactive accident or emergency, which were confirmed in 2012 by the expert group.

in writing. the report considers that the european 'cultural and creative industries' are a driver of economic growth and job creation, a subsidiary reasoning of the commercialisation of culture and knowledge, which we do not see. it notes that some 39% of eu economic activity, worth around €4.7 billion per year, is generated by ipr-intensive sectors, which also create 26% of direct jobs (i.e. 56 million jobs), representing indirect employment plus 9% of the total number of jobs in the eu. the report defends the public domain and involves the internet operators in the problem, points with which we agree. it advocates limiting the use of works, considers private property to be a pillar of creativity and, with regard to private copying, advocates the harmonisation of regimes but does not clarify in what sense. these are things we disagree on. as regards the so-called 'freedom of panorama', we believe that prior authorisation by the authors of the works should not be required, even for commercial use. what is needed is that the copyright be paid to them, but not that the authors give prior information.
in writing. ‒ i welcome the rejection of the epp amendment which sought to restrict the freedom of street photography, or panorama photography. although this is an own-initiative report, without binding force, to include such an amendment, contrary to what its authors intended, would send the committee a completely wrong signal as to which way to legislate. however, the inclusion of several other proposals from the right which distort the original report and the balance between copyright and consumer rights led me to abstain.
‒ i voted in favour of the report on the harmonisation of certain aspects of copyright and related rights in the information society. given that the european cultural and creative industries are a driver of economic growth and job creation, employing more than 7 million people and generating more than 4,2% of the european union's gdp, it is imperative to harmonise, within the european area, all aspects necessary for the effective protection of the rights of authors of literary and artistic works, in order to reflect the technological developments operating in this market.
‒ i agree that the revision of directive 2001/29/ec is essential for the promotion of creativity and innovation, cultural diversity, economic growth, competitiveness, the digital single market and access to knowledge and information, while at the same time granting authors of literary and artistic works sufficient recognition and protection of their rights. i support the european cultural and creative industries as a driver of economic growth and job creation in the eu and as making an important contribution to the eu economy, and therefore vote in favour of this report. i would also stress the importance of authors being paid fairly by producers, and being paid fairly and in accordance with the verified digital views. i also think it is unacceptable that there should be a restriction on the freedom to take photographs of public buildings when they are used for non-commercial purposes.
‒ the purpose of this resolution is to adapt copyright and related rights legislation to new technologies, in particular the information society, and to implement the international obligations arising from the two treaties adopted under the auspices of the world intellectual property organisation (wipo) in december 1996. the resolution sets out a set of recommendations for legislative reform that the commission should present by the end of the year, precisely to modernise legislation, making it more compatible with the new digital age we are living in. the report deals with the new rules on the right of reproduction, the right of communication to the public and the right of distribution, which i agree with, and also deals with issues such as geo-blocking, the promotion of creativity and the remuneration of rights holders. a final point to mention is that i voted against the freedom of panorama provision, because i do not think it acceptable that the commercial use of photographs, video images or other images of works which are permanently displayed in public physical places always requires the prior authorization of their authors.
‒ i respect and admire artistic creation and believe that it should enjoy a legislative context that both promotes and defends it. the digital platforms have presented a challenge in that the balance between remunerating artists and democratizing access to artistic production needs to be struck. i believe that a new approach to copyright is urgently needed to address this new reality, without restricting the rights of access and sharing of citizens in general. i regret that it was not possible to vote and approve the concept of an inalienable right to remuneration subject to collective management.
in writing. the report stresses that european cultural and creative industries are a driver of economic growth and job creation in the eu and make an important contribution to the eu economy, employing over 7 million people and generating over 4,2% of eu gdp, according to the latest estimates, and whereas cultural industries continued to create jobs during the 2008-2012 economic crisis. the report defends the public domain and involves the internet operators in the problem, points with which we agree. it supports the limitation of the use of works, considers private property to be a pillar of creativity and, as regards private copying, supports the harmonization of regimes but does not clarify in what sense, aspects with which we do not agree. it emphasises the importance of libraries for access to knowledge, advocating the adoption of exceptions that legally allow public and research libraries to lend digital works to the public for personal use via the internet or library networks, as well as to digitize content for consultation, cataloguing and archiving purposes, and authors should receive fair compensation for digital content lending equivalent to that received for physical book lending, in accordance with national territorial restrictions.
‒ there are several points on which we agree in this report, namely the defence of the public domain and the involvement of internet operators in the problem. the report also stresses the importance of libraries for access to knowledge, advocating the adoption of exceptions that legally allow public and research libraries to lend digital works to the public for personal use via the internet or library networks, as well as to digitize content for consultation, cataloguing and archiving purposes, which is important to ensure more equal access to knowledge. we voted against the part of the text which requires prior authorization from authors for the use of works in the public domain, because we feel that this should not be necessary. however, we do not agree with a perspective that places the users of cultural content as the main responsible for the remuneration of authors, which should fall mainly on the platforms that profit from the provision of this content. we therefore do not agree with perspectives that limit content sharing or with claims that "glorify" private property as a higher principle to be defended. we abstained.

‒ forced labour is a violation of human rights and an attack on the dignity of millions of women, men, girls and boys. in the 21st century, forced labor affects 21 million people, victims of an exploitation that generates $150 billion a year in income for the benefit of those who organize and manage it. although debt slavery no longer officially exists on the european continent, 880 000 people in the european union and 1.6 million across the continent are affected by these new forms of forced labour. men and women who have been offered jobs abroad are deceived by their alleged employers, just as migrants are deceived by smugglers, and children are made vulnerable by uprooting. labour rights are therefore a fundamental pillar of decent work and constitute the main instrument in the fight against labour exploitation. the protocol calls on governments to take measures to better protect workers, in particular migrant workers, from abusive and fraudulent recruitment practices.

in writing. ‒ we are dealing with a request for the waiver of the parliamentary immunity of a member of the european parliament, which arises following a request by a judicial authority to bring a judicial action against him, relating to infringements of the road traffic code. it has been established that the alleged acts are not directly related to the exercise of his parliamentary functions, nor is there even a presumption that the proceedings were instituted for political reasons, which is why i subscribe to the position taken in this decision, having voted in favour of the request for the waiver of the parliamentary immunity of janusz korwin-mikke.
‒ member of parliament janusz korwin-mikke is accused of driving a vehicle at excessive speed in a residential area in piotrków trybunalski on 6 september 2014. according to police records, he was driving at 50 miles an hour when the speed limit is 30 miles an hour. this conduct constitutes an offence under article 92a of the polish law. in addition to the vehicle being registered in the mp's name, the police claim that the facial image of the driver, visible in the photograph recorded by the speed recording camera, matches the facial image of the mp. the acts alleged have no direct or obvious connection with the performance of the duties of a member of the european parliament, nor do they constitute opinions or votes expressed in the performance of his duties as a member of the european parliament. we voted to lift parliamentary immunity.

‒ action against breaches of customs rules is essential for the protection of the union's financial interests and the development of customs cooperation. customs regulations may be infringed by various practices such as misleading description of imported goods in order to benefit from reduced duties, misleading declaration of origin of goods in order to circumvent anti-dumping duties and/or to avoid quantitative limitations or import quotas, or misuse of the transit procedure where the goods actually imported are declared in transit in order to avoid the applicable customs duties. we must avoid these practices, which is why i am voting in favour.
‒ currently, customs officials have no mechanisms to verify that the declared origin of the goods is in accordance with the route of the container in question and there is abuse of the transit procedure which is monitored through documentary and visual checks of limited scope. i would point out that false declarations of origin represent an annual loss of eur 100 million for the eu and, as regards the misleading description of the products transported, the losses reported by the member states in 2011 were around eur 107.7 million. i agree with the importance of speeding up the mechanisms for combating customs fraud and avoiding red tape, thereby strengthening the security of the internal market and the products circulating therein, and also ensuring greater protection for consumers. i would stress that, given the fact that some shortcomings have been identified in the e-customs system, it is essential to amend it in order to make the procedure quicker and less bureaucratic.
i voted against because i disagree with the council's position.
‒ the commission proposes to amend regulation (ec) no 515/97 with a view to improving the detection, investigation and prevention of customs fraud by increasing the exchange of information and available evidence. there is an objective need for greater cooperation and action in this area, particularly in creating conditions for a better fight against customs fraud, especially in relation to the misrepresentation of the origin of goods and abusive practices in the transit system. i believe that the options presented are in line with fundamental rights and will not only allow for a stronger legal framework but also for greater exchange of information on container movements and transit, import and export data. that is why i voted in favour of this proposal.
‒ every effort should be made to ensure that controls on agricultural products imported from third countries are effective. effectiveness in this context implies checking the origin of the products so that it is possible to ascertain their production conditions and compliance with established trade agreements. this is the starting point for ensuring reciprocity in production standards and protecting the competitive conditions of european agricultural producers.
‒ the fight against fraud in the context of the customs union and the common agricultural policy is at the heart of this regulation, which requires close cooperation between the administrative authorities responsible in each member state for implementing the provisions adopted in these two areas. it also requires appropriate cooperation between these national authorities and the commission, which is responsible for ensuring the application of the treaty and the provisions adopted pursuant to it, implying effective cooperation in this field which can strengthen the protection of the community's financial interests.
‒ the european parliament and the council adopted in 2009 a regulation on trade in seal products, which prohibits this practice in the european union and applies to seal products produced in the eu and to imported products. the eu has opted for a 'total' ban, with two main exceptions. given that the objective of the new regulation is to implement the wto recommendations and decisions on the 2009 basic regulation on trade in seal products, i agree with the deletion of the gmr exception and the proposed amendment with regard to the ci exception, taking into account in particular the right to self-determination of inuit or other indigenous communities. i also agree with the amendment proposed to insist that seal hunting is an integral part of the culture and identity of inuit and other indigenous communities, contributing significantly to their livelihood, providing food and income that allows the community to live and sustain its livelihood, perpetuating its traditions and preserving its cultural heritage, of which direct trade is part.
‒ the purpose of this legislative proposal is to implement the recommendations and decisions of the era in relation to the basic regulation. it also establishes the legal basis for the co-ordination of regulation (eu) no 737/2010 with those decisions. the reservations regarding the met exception are addressed by deleting it from the basic regulation. in the case of the ci exception, the reservations as to its design and application are addressed by amending it, inter alia by linking its use with respect for animal welfare and by providing for a limit on the placing on the market of seal products if the scale of the hunt or other circumstances indicate that it has primarily commercial purposes. that is why i am voting in favour.
‒ i am in favour of a total ban on trade in seal products, except in the two situations presented: a) ci exception - products derived from seals hunted by inuit or other indigenous communities; b) gmr exception - products of hunting carried out for the sole purpose of ensuring the sustainable management of small-scale and non-profit-making marine resources. as regards the first exception, my position is justified by the fact that seal hunting is a cultural tradition of inuit and other indigenous communities, contributing to their subsistence, providing food and income. as regards the second exception, given the difficulty of distinguishing between commercial hunting and gmr hunting, i argue that it can only be carried out in very specific circumstances, allowing this exception for the management of marine resources to fulfil its objective of promoting the protection of natural biodiversity. i therefore voted in favour of this report.

‒ this report proposes new rules to prohibit the cloning of all animal species for farming purposes and the import of food and other products, such as semen and embryos, from these animals or their descendants. the aim is to address animal health and welfare concerns, consumer perceptions and ethical considerations related to the cloning technique. i believe that these rules should apply to all species of animals kept and bred for farming purposes, and not just to cattle, pigs, sheep, goats and equidae, as the commission proposal provides.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour because, apart from all the ethical issues, i believe that there is no need to resort to cloning animals for food purposes. we need to think about a sustainable approach to farming and not leave our food to the interests of multinationals and big industry. the use of clones for agricultural purposes not only poses a threat to food security and animal health and welfare, but will also have incalculable consequences for the environment and biodiversity. we cannot allow these products to enter the market and reach consumers.
‒ the aim of this proposal is to ensure uniform production conditions for farmers while protecting animal health and welfare.
‒ i agree that the negative effects of cloning, particularly on animal welfare, outweigh any possible positive effects. at present, animal cloning for agricultural purposes does not take place in the european union. the commission has proposed bans on the placing on the market of animal clones and the marketing of food derived from animal clones, but these have been contrary to our reality, since the cloning technique is quite expensive, with a low success rate and little profit in food production. i agree with the rapporteurs that the main concerns relating to cloning, namely the production of germ products (semen, oocytes and embryos) from clones for use in animal reproduction by conventional reproduction techniques, have not been addressed. i would point out that the cloning technique is permitted in some third countries, such as the usa, canada, argentina, brazil and australia. it would be contradictory to ban the cloning technique in the eu, for scientific and ethical reasons, and to continue to allow the import of the main products for which the technique is mainly used, such as germinal products derived from clones and food derived from clone offspring.

in writing. ‒ in december 2013, the commission published two legislative proposals on the cloning of animals for food purposes - the one currently under consideration and a follow-up proposal to the directive on the placing on the market of foodstuffs derived from cloned animals. both aim to suspend the use of the cloning technique in the eu for farmed animals, the placing on the market of live animal clones and clones in the embryonic stage, and the marketing of foodstuffs, such as meat and milk, derived from animal clones. i agree with the rapporteur's position on the negative effects of cloning and i support the commission's proposal. however, there are a number of concerns raised by citizens and the european parliament that have not been addressed, in particular with regard to food derived from the offspring of cloned animals and the reproductive material of clones and their offspring. i therefore support the amendments tabled by the rapporteurs to strengthen the commission's proposal to create a coherent and effective regulation which responds to the legitimate concerns of the agricultural sector and of european citizens in general and which is compatible with the wto regulatory framework.
in writing. - science should serve humanity, but within ethical parameters. cloning for food production poses too many problems in terms of animal welfare for such a practice to be justified today. for this reason, it should be opposed outright. while it is also true that this practice does not represent any economic advantage, there are countries where animals descended from cloned animals enter the food chain. on the other hand, the use of cloned reproductive material for animal breeding purposes is also common. it is important to establish an absolutely rigorous and reliable traceability system for the importation into the european union of animals descended from cloned animals and of cloned genetic material.

in writing. the severe economic and financial crisis that has hit the eu in recent years has also given rise to a serious social crisis that has worsened the living conditions of millions of europeans. as a citizen of a country which has applied for a financial assistance programme, i wish to express my regret by my vote at the lack of democratic control over the measures implemented in this context, particularly as regards respect for the principle of subsidiarity. the programmes were implemented often at the expense of the fundamental values and rights enshrined in the treaties and european union law, which in turn undermined the trust of the citizens in their representatives, including the european parliament. i fully endorse the call in this report for the commission to assume its role of overseeing the full and proper application of the laws in order to protect fundamental rights and, together with the council and the member states, to ensure that the fundamental principles and rights of citizens are respected in economic and social matters and with regard to, among others, equality and non-discrimination, freedom of expression, religion and conscience, the protection of minorities and the rights of migrants and applicants for international protection.
‒ the ferrara report focuses on fundamental rights, which are the deepest foundation of the ideals and values on which the european union is based. this exercise which the european parliament carries out every year is only useful if it gives us a picture of reality which enables us to identify our areas of action. but the fundamental rights in this house should unite and not divide. the ferrara report goes too far. it goes beyond questionable censorship considerations and often goes beyond the scope of the union's powers. and it proposes a mechanism that certainly should not be discussed here. changing the nature of the eu and the distinction between what is european and what is national is a matter for the treaties. for all these reasons, i abstained in the final vote, although i agree with many of the points in the report.
‒ the document addresses issues such as the impact of austerity measures on economic, civil, social and cultural rights, the rights of refugees, children and lgbti people, discrimination, corruption and violations of press freedom. i therefore support the existence of a permanent monitoring mechanism for the respect of fundamental rights by all eu countries. the report deals with a number of violations which i consider to be of priority in the light of the current political situation, such as freedom of expression, the need to ensure a fair balance between respect for fundamental rights and the guarantee of collective security, and the impact of austerity policies and corruption on fundamental rights.
‒ the eu, which so often makes recommendations on the violation of human rights by third countries, cannot but look at itself and examine whether and to what extent fundamental rights are being respected within its own borders. situations such as the recent humanitarian crisis of migrants and refugees and the stance of some member states, such as hungary, show how much remains to be done. it is essential to have an additional mechanism to enhance effective respect for and protection of the fundamental rights of individuals against violations of those rights, including the right to effective remedies, and to enhance the accountability of the european institutions for their actions or omissions in this area. i share the concern about the worrying trend in the violation of fundamental rights in the eu, particularly in the field of immigration and asylum, about discrimination and intolerance against certain populations and about attacks or pressure on ngos defending the rights of these groups and populations. i regret the reluctance of member states to enforce the fundamental freedoms and rights that assist roma, women, lgbti people, asylum seekers, migrants and other vulnerable populations. for all these reasons, i voted in favour.

‒ respect for and promotion of human rights, fundamental freedoms, democracy and the values and principles enshrined in the eu treaties and international rights instruments must be at the heart of the european construction and its policies. in accordance with article 2 teu, the union is founded on the values of respect for human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and respect for human rights, including the rights of persons belonging to minorities, which are common to all the member states. in this regard, and although i disagree with some of the wording in this report, i consider it absolutely essential that these rights are guaranteed to all persons living in the territory of the eu, including against abuses and acts of violence by public authorities, and are defended by the eu and each member state in all its policies, both internally and externally, and to this end it is necessary to make full use of existing mechanisms to ensure respect for, the protection and promotion of fundamental rights and the values on which the union is founded.
in writing. ‒ unfortunately, we continue to see numerous and alarming violations of fundamental rights on the territory of the member states of the european union. this is unacceptable and the european institutions and the member states must react firmly and forcefully to prevent and put an end to these violations. i therefore support the rapporteur's proposal for the creation of an internal eu strategy for fundamental rights in the member states, as well as a mechanism to deter and eradicate violations within the eu and its application in external relations.
‒ the charter of fundamental rights recognises a range of personal, civil, political, economic and social rights for eu citizens and residents. the report proposes the formulation of an internal eu strategy on fundamental rights, which ensures respect for european values as enshrined in article 2 of the tfeu and the eu charter of fundamental rights. the commission proposes that an internal strategy be developed and that a mechanism be set up to prevent and eliminate violations of fundamental rights in the member states. however, there are two fundamental problems: firstly, the fact that the strategy would involve the creation of a complementary mechanism for assessing the respect of fundamental rights in europe, which would require a revision of the treaties, thus making it manifestly disproportionate and unworkable; secondly, the disregard of the principle of subsidiarity, denying member states competence in matters of family law and also in the security issues mentioned in the report, where the commission has limited rights to intervene, as this is a competence exclusively of the member states. in view of the foregoing and as this is a legislative resolution on the situation of fundamental rights in the european union, i have decided to abstain from voting on this resolution.
in writing. ‒ this report looks at the situation of fundamental rights in the eu in 2013 and 2014 and is part of a particularly favourable and sensitive institutional context for respect for fundamental rights in the european union today. although it points out relevant aspects, and in some cases it does so with certainty, it does not point to the social and labour attacks which millions of workers are suffering in countries where austerity policies are making their way. it also omits the role of the european union in the destruction of countries such as libya, syria and iraq, where the aim is to secure control of raw materials and energy sources. in this sense, the report is a mere exercise in diversion and in whitewashing the role of the eu and its imperialist and oppressive policy.

‒ public hearings of potential members of the european commission are a valuable exercise. these hearings provide an opportunity for parliament and the public to assess the personalities, general approach and priorities of each candidate commissioner and their qualifications. although not provided for in the treaties, they are a practice developed over the last 20 years at the insistence of parliament, which simply required candidate commissioners to appear for a hearing before the competent parliamentary committees before parliament gave its vote of confidence to the commission. although the emphasis is on whether or not a commissioner has been rejected, this process generates other developments such as clarifications and political commitments, a better definition of the portfolios and some additional clarifications on the issue of relations between vice-presidents and other commissioners. these hearings increase the democratic legitimacy of the union's institutions by bringing them closer to the european citizens.
‒ public hearings of potential members of the european commission are a valuable exercise. the procedure for hearings is not provided for in the treaty. it is a practice developed over the last 20 years, at the insistence of parliament, which simply required candidate commissioners to appear for a hearing before the parliamentary committees of their respective countries before parliament gave its vote of confidence to the commission. the hearings are obviously not an opportunity to try to change the political composition of the commission, which reflects the political balance between national governments and not that of parliament. any candidate rejected shall be replaced by another, appointed by the same government. i agree that there is always room for improvement and that there should be an evaluation of procedures and methods and a reflection on lessons that can be learned to improve the process next time.

in writing. ‒ the importance of technologies in the functioning of our societies is now indisputable. technologies empower the individual and empower free communities. in countries that are still without democracy, this effect is even more evident, as was evident with the arab spring. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to cover the whole of the european union, including the european union's neighbours. on the other hand, new technologies have also given the states more ways of monitoring and controlling. used effectively and legally, these are new tools to combat terrorism, corruption or child pornography. however, they are also weapons of censorship, tracking or surveillance on a large scale. snowden's revelations have shown us how these new tools can, in fact, lead to unimaginable abuses. in a society where new technologies can threaten fundamental freedoms, public authorities are required not to compromise on the debauchery of police or secret services without authorisation and judicial review.

‒ this report focuses on how technological advances play a key role in ensuring respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. i would stress that technology can have a positive effect on human rights by extending the scope of freedom of expression, access to information and the right to privacy and freedom of assembly and association worldwide. on the other hand, it also has a harmful side when used for human rights violations through censorship, surveillance, unauthorized access to devices and the tracking of information and people. i support the concerns reflected in this report, such as the need to ensure coherence between the eu's external actions and its internal policies related to ict. i also believe that the impact of technology on improving human rights should be integrated into all eu policies and programmes. support the promotion of best practices and appropriate legislative frameworks, while ensuring the security and integrity of personal data. i advocate the promotion and use of free and open source software and encryption technologies, and support for the removal of digital barriers for people with disabilities.
‒ technological developments play an important role in ensuring the exercise and respect of human rights and fundamental freedoms. when misused, however, technological systems can be tools for human rights violations. it is therefore important to strike the right balance between digital freedom and digital security. in this context, the report calls on the eu and the member states to actively promote the global use and creation of open standards and free and open source software and encryption technologies; stresses the need for communication surveillance to be subject to an appropriate legal framework; regrets that some eu information and communication technologies and services are sold in third countries with the intention of violating human rights; and calls for the inclusion of conditionality clauses in agreements with third countries, which refer to the need to guarantee digital freedoms, net neutrality, uncensored internet access and privacy and data protection. although i agree in principle with the aims and concerns expressed in the report, i believe that some of the wording is subordinating the issues of the security of citizens and the institutions in terms that i cannot follow.
‒ human rights and fundamental freedoms are universal and must be defended on a global scale in all dimensions of their expression. new technologies can enhance our freedoms, but they can also be used to interfere with privacy and freedom of expression if they are carried out outside an appropriate legal framework. digital freedoms, net neutrality and unlimited access to the internet, but also privacy and data protection (in eu countries and in their relations with third countries) need to be promoted, guaranteed and respected. that is the direction taken by the report by marietje schaake.
‒ this own-initiative report expresses very valid concerns about the use of information and communication technologies (ict) as a pretext to violate the right to privacy and to repress legitimate activities by citizens/groups of citizens in third countries, and also highlights the impact this perception may have on citizens' overall confidence in the use of ict. it also states that some of these icts are sold and used in third countries, not only by authorities, but also by individuals or companies that violate the most basic fundamental rights, although there are no concrete data. while i think that this report has some virtuous ideas, i think it is somewhat biased, not particularly highlighting the fundamental security and defence matrix of icts and their help in preventing/early detection of potential terrorist attacks against innocent victims. moreover, the specific conditioning provided for in point 17 may be misinterpreted by the third countries concerned and confused with 'ex-colonial paternalism', which is completely unacceptable to some. contrary to this idea, i believe that the eu's focus should be on the defence of human rights in general. the epp also tried to negotiate a text which it considered more balanced, but without success. for all these reasons, i voted against.
‒ technological developments and unlimited access to the open internet play an increasingly important role in enabling and ensuring the exercise and full respect of human rights and fundamental freedoms. there is a positive effect of these technological developments, expanding the scope of freedom of expression, access to information and the right to privacy and freedom of assembly and association worldwide. all these positive aspects, among many others, force us, however, to examine the limits of the use of these same technologies, in particular the impact of intrusion and surveillance systems on human rights in third countries. i voted in favour of this report and stress the need to ensure democratic scrutiny of digital surveillance processes in accordance with international law, through appropriate parliamentary, executive and, in particular, judicial supervision. privacy and individual liberty cannot be infringed, except in extreme cases, duly justified and scrutinized by international justice.
‒ the report considers that technological developments and unlimited access to the open internet play an increasingly important role in enabling and ensuring the exercise and full respect of human rights and fundamental freedoms, with a positive effect by expanding the scope of freedom of expression, access to information and the right to privacy and freedom of assembly and association worldwide. it also considers that technological systems can be misused as tools for human rights violations through censorship, surveillance, unauthorised access to devices, obstruction, interception and the tracking and tracing of information and people. however, it says nothing about the control of these means and the need for such control to be public, as the only way to guarantee universal access and prevent abuses.
in writing. ‒ in the two phases of the reform of the common agricultural policy (cap), the rules have become more diverse and complex, leading to more errors on the ground. given that the objectives of the cap must be met and that mutual understanding and trust between all eu institutions and national and regional bodies must be ensured for its effective implementation, a more effective and efficient cap reform requires simplification and less red tape to achieve its objectives. the costs of controls and advice to stakeholders and farmers currently amount to eur 4 billion per year at member state level and are likely to increase. i believe and agree that a less bureaucratic cap is needed to reduce the error rate and to create instruments which allow the distinction between error and fraud to be made.
‒ in the two phases of the reform of the common agricultural policy (cap), the rules have become more diverse and complex. more complex rules lead to more errors in the field. the cap needs to be less bureaucratic, to reduce the error rate, and to create instruments which allow the distinction between error and fraud to be made. only then will the eu's financial interests be effectively safeguarded. that is why i am voting in favour.
‒ the reform of the common agricultural policy has made the rules more diverse and complex, resulting in more errors on the ground and an increase in administrative burdens. i am in favour of greater simplification and less red tape for the common agricultural policy, which is intended to be effective and efficient. i believe that the objectives of the cap must be met and that mutual understanding and trust between all the eu institutions and national and regional bodies must be ensured for its effective implementation. i think it is essential that the complexity of the systems and application forms for farmers be reduced. i stress the importance of sharing experience between best and worst performing member states, as well as communication between national and regional authorities and their joint work in an articulated and efficient way for the benefit of farmers implementing the policy on the ground. i agree with the rapporteur that a single audit should be more firmly implemented by coordinating the control activities carried out by the various institutions, so that farmers are not subject to different visits by the competent bodies at different times in the same year.
i voted in favour because i believe it is essential that there should be strict financial control of the cap's performance.
‒ the verification of 50 million transactions and other cap controls costs about four billion euros a year. given that the provisions for cap expenditure for the period 2014-2020 remain complex, the costs of monitoring the €58 billion cap budget are expected to grow further if nothing is done. i therefore share the view that a financial balance must be found, capable of reducing administrative burdens and ensuring more effective financial control, as well as fully reliable first-level controls and the provision of credible data by the member states, so that they do not have to be duplicated at eu level. i am in favour of the objective of implementing the single audit scheme with only one audit chain, simplifying the process. i also agree with risk-based controls, where the best performing member states should be rewarded with a reduction in union controls. i would also stress as a positive aspect the sharing and exchange of good practice, in order to ensure more fluid controls and the least possible disturbance of farmers' activities.
‒ public funding implies a control logic that must be proportionate to the risks of infringement. in turn, the rules governing the use of public money should be sufficiently clear and adapted to reality so that beneficiaries and implementing bodies can contribute to the good implementation of the funding possibilities. only then can the policy objectives be successfully implemented. the agricultural funds have been relatively well implemented under the structural funds and this is an interesting prospect. farmers are now in the grip of the implementation of the latest reform of the common agricultural policy, with new rules to apply. we expect the support of the european and national authorities to ensure that our farmers continue to benefit from support, as well as the flexibility needed to take account of this new legislative reality.
‒ despite the supposed simplification of the cap, the truth is that farmers still face an endless mountain of paperwork that has to be submitted, with increasingly complex regulations and control measures. the promotion of performance-based controls can be an answer to some of these questions, and this report insists that the definition of performance in relation to controls should primarily imply the quality of member states' administrative controls and systems, i.e. the efficiency, consistency and reliability of the managing and certifying authorities. we agree that in order to reduce the burden on beneficiaries, operators should not be burdened with a disproportionate number of inspections.
‒ we follow the concerns expressed both in opinion no 1/2012 of the european court of auditors on certain proposals for regulations relating to the common agricultural policy and in this report about the complexity of the supposedly simplified common agricultural policy. what has happened with this supposed simplification of the cap is that farmers still face enormous bureaucracy. we agree that in order to reduce the burden on beneficiaries, and considering that it is important not to burden operators with a disproportionate number of inspections, the authorities should aim to organise on-the-spot checks so as not to subject the farmer to multiple annual on-the-spot checks by the national authorities, the commission or the court of auditors. we have serious reservations about the creation of a list of good and bad compliers, as opposed to a 'black list' which discriminates against countries where small farmers do not have the capacity to comply with all the controls required by a deeply bureaucratic and complex cap.

‒ being european also means recognising and valuing difference and diversity. the valorisation and promotion of tangible and intangible cultural heritage is a factor of enormous importance for european integration. it is also a way of deepening knowledge and consequently of making the most of local specificities. it can also be a decisive factor in making europe a more differentiated tourist destination. it therefore deserves an integrated and inclusive approach by the commission, the council and the member states, capable of exploiting europe's immense cultural potential. the report under consideration is intended above all to respond to the needs and desires expressed by those who deal with this phenomenon on a daily basis and who have difficulties in accessing information and funding. the proposals which propose concrete measures to deal with these difficulties are therefore timely. the revision of governance models is another measure that can make a difference. the cultural phenomenon is not, and fortunately it is not, immune to new organizational models, which is why these deserve particular attention.
in writing. ‒ we do not intend to give way to the commercialisation of cultural heritage and the defence of public-private partnerships. we support some proposals, such as the creation of a single eu portal dedicated to cultural heritage, which would bring together information on all eu funding programmes geared to cultural heritage, the increase of the €5 million ceiling for investment projects in small-scale infrastructure, the creation of a policy framework for the historic-patrimonial real estate environment, which would contain a regulatory framework for monuments and archaeological and historic landscapes. we do not follow the meaning of the designation 'european union heritage' given on the basis of the mere location of the heritage elements in question, since as is known, the 'european' heritage is indebted to many cultures and could also be claimed by others geographically outside the european continent. this designation is based on the development of the fallacy of the existence of a unique european identity and culture, in 'european' values, entering into a particularly sensitive area about which we have serious reservations.

‒ the human right to water and sanitation is essential for the full enjoyment of life and all other human rights. all people should have access to water in good quality and quantity (as well as to basic sanitation). i regret that in the eu more than one million people do not have regular access to drinking water, and an estimated 10 million citizens do not have access to sanitation. for all these reasons, the vote against this report was excluded. however, the right to water cannot mean that water services should be free. the tariffs should cover the resource and the operational costs of the service, but should also allow companies to invest in infrastructure, improving the service provided to citizens. although water is a public good, the choice of how to manage water services is subject to the principle of subsidiarity and is the responsibility of national and local authorities, reflecting the diversity of european traditions and models. the report's inclination towards a model which is contrary to this view therefore prevents my vote in favour, and i shall therefore abstain in the final vote, as it has not been possible, in the field of speciality, to purge the most collectivist points of the report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour and i am pleased that a european institution has finally recognised the right to water as a fundamental right. but this report, in addition to recognising the human right to water and sanitation, calls on the commission to discourage water grabbing and fracking (shale gas exploitation) and recognises that water and sanitation services are services of general interest, that water is a common good and therefore must be made available at affordable prices that respect citizens' rights to a minimum quality of water. it also includes several recommendations to the european commission to exclude water and sanitation services from any international agreements and, in the case of the transatlantic trade and investment partnership (ttip) and the trade and services agreement (tisa), the imperative to establish a legally binding exclusion clause for these same services. there is still a long way to go before this is an effective right, but this first institutional step, following the first step taken by citizens who signed up to the european citizens' initiative, is a clear signpost for the way forward for the other institutions.
‒ the european citizens' initiative has been available since 1 april 2012 as a new mechanism for participatory democracy. the european commission has stated that it would like citizens to take a more active role in the european political process, and this unique instrument is designed to allow eu citizens to directly influence and shape the european political agenda. under the rules on the european citizens' initiative, it needs at least one million signatures in at least seven member states to be presented. european citizens' initiative water and sanitation are a human right! water is not a commercial good, but a public good!, also known as right2water, has, at the time of its launch, collected over 1.6 million verified signatures, which have since been joined by almost 300,000. it managed to collect signatures from all member states and exceeded the minimum required in 13 member states, thus becoming the first successful european citizens' initiative.
