‒ the current rules governing package holidays are clearly outdated in the face of the new realities of the digital age and the changing paradigm in the travel market. european consumers were less protected, as existing standards either did not provide for these situations or covered them in a vague way, as they were designed only for traditional package travel. the current status quo of non-application to online travel and the fragmented legislation of the member states to regulate it creates uncertainty for consumers about their rights, as well as uncertainty for operators about their responsibilities and fragmentation of the internal market. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the transport of dangerous goods by road, rail and inland waterway. consumers must be at the centre of the internal market, and greater transparency and increased consumer protection are now recognised on the one hand, and the desired harmonisation that provides fairness for businesses on the other.
‒ the package travel directive dates back to 1990 and is drawn up taking into account the fact that the vast majority of europeans book their holidays through travel agencies rather than the internet. it was important to update the directive to adapt it to the digital age and to strengthen consumer rights, such as the right to terminate the contract if the price increase exceeds 8%, to be repatriated if the tour operator goes bankrupt and to receive assistance if something goes wrong during the holiday. personalised travel is not covered by the rules in force or is ambiguously covered, leaving consumers unsure of their rights and operators unsure of their exact obligations. this update means that an additional 120 million consumers who buy these personalised travel packages will also be protected, according to european commission data.
in the light of the above, the commission considers that the proposed directive should be amended to include the following elements: the european commission proposes that the operator be allowed to increase the price in line with fuel costs, taxes and exchange rate fluctuations, which clearly puts the consumer in a vulnerable position. in addition, the organiser/retailer is obliged to provide protection in the event of insolvency in order to guarantee the repatriation of travellers and the reimbursement of payments made. however, this obligation only applies to package travel organisers and retailers offering the purchase of combined travel services. the proposal does, however, solve some of the existing problems, since the directive is outdated, given the emergence of digital operators, which creates disadvantageous conditions for many smes in the sector. that is why, even if this proposal is not entirely positive, in its current form, which deserves the agreement of the council and the european commission, we voted against the proposal of the efdd group to reject, outright, the amendment of the directive, which would make it impossible to improve the current situation.
‒ the european parliament has approved the revision of the package travel directive (created in 1990). this legislative update is of great relevance in an increasingly digital age, where consumers book more and more trips online. it is essential that there is a stronger enforcement and monitoring of consumer rights in balance with the protection of freedom of movement.
in writing. the revision of the 1990 directive on package travel and related travel services was adopted today. this recommendation for second reading on the council's position at first reading adapts this directive to the digital age and the fact that 60% of consumers book and buy their holidays online. travellers using the internet will now be more protected in their contract and should also have an emergency telephone number or a point of contact with the organiser or travel agency. the strengthening of their consumer rights also covers issues of receiving assistance if something goes wrong during the holiday, being repatriated in the event of the tour operator's bankruptcy and terminating the contract if the price increase is more than 8%. i voted in favour of this proposal, which member states must transpose into national law within two years, with the new rules coming into force six months later.
‒ i voted in favour of the proposal because i believe it is important to harmonise the rights and obligations arising from package travel contracts and related travel services in order to create a genuine internal market for consumers in this field.
‒ tourism and, more specifically, travel, including the related sectors, accounts for around 10% of the eu's gross domestic product. the adoption in 1990 of directive 90/314/eec on package holidays recognised the importance of the rights of european travellers when they purchased package holidays, typically consisting of transport and accommodation. however, we are in 2015 - the digital age and with a different and much more complex transport market structure than in 1990, when the internet practically did not exist. with the widespread use of air travel and the liberalisation of air transport, it has become essential to revise the directive, giving greater clarity and breadth to its content and scope, as well as greater protection for european consumers in respect of this segment of package travel and related travel services. in concrete terms, i stress the need for measures to adapt to the digital age, for assistance and repatriation rights in the event of bankruptcy, for the termination of contracts in the event of an unjustified price increase, and i therefore support this report which, in addition to supporting an urgent revision of the directive, also promotes the harmonisation of the internal market in regulatory terms and ensures the defence and protection of consumers and businesses.
‒ the aim is to ensure that the traveller, when purchasing linked travel services, is protected in the event of the insolvency of the operator providing the linked travel service. the traveller will therefore have the right to be repatriated if the insolvency of the operator responsible for the carriage of passengers causes the traveller to be stranded at his destination. moreover, before concluding the contract giving rise to the related service, the operator must inform the traveller, using standard forms, that he will not benefit from the rights guaranteed by the directive, except for protection against insolvency. these are positive elements, but they do not touch on the real problem of private monopolies in the field of transport, which have taken over the public service and have become a drain on public resources to the detriment of the quality and universality of the service.
in the light of the above, the commission considers that the proposed directive should be amended to include a new provision on the protection of consumers in the context of the provision of services. the european commission proposes that the operator has the right to increase the price in line with fuel costs, taxes and exchange rate fluctuations, which clearly puts the consumer in a very vulnerable position. in addition, the organiser/retailer is obliged to provide protection in the event of insolvency in order to guarantee the repatriation of travellers and the reimbursement of payments made. however, this obligation only applies to package travel organisers and retailers offering the purchase of combined travel services. although the proposal on the table from the european council and the european commission is not entirely positive, particularly for those who buy travel, we voted against the proposal from the efdd group to reject the amendment of the directive, a directive which is obsolete in view of the emergence of digital operators and which puts smes in the sector at a disadvantage.
‒ i share the disappointment of so many who would have preferred clearer wording on net neutrality. however, the provisions of article 3 (3) on the treatment of traffic establish principles of equality and non-discrimination which i subscribe to. rejecting the compromise reached between parliament and the council would mean three things: 1) returning to the '0' point and waiting a few more years for a new directive; 2) no european standard in the meantime (with the market fragmented into 28 national legal orders... now, the digital internal market calls for legal certainty and harmonisation of standards); 3) rejecting other positive points in the same legal act, such as the end of roaming, which, if the directive is rejected, would continue for several years. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter.
‒ i voted in favour of the text agreed by the european parliament and the council of the european union in the trilogues last june, because i consider that the end of roaming charges is a great victory for the european project and also a great victory for citizens living in border regions or who have to travel frequently to other member states of the union. in addition to the reduction of roaming charges in 2016 and their abolition in 2017, a very important aspect for the internal market is the establishment of open internet access throughout the eu territory, without blocking or slowing down the quality of the signal due to the location or the type of data being exchanged by the user, something that is certainly of great importance to europeans.
in writing. the new telecoms market regulation includes the first provisions at european level to safeguard open access to the internet by requiring operators to treat all traffic fairly when providing online services. roaming surcharges charged when a person uses his mobile phone in another eu country to make calls, send sms or access the internet will be abolished on 15 june 2017. however, when roaming exceeds the limits of reasonable use, a small fee may be charged. this fee may not exceed the maximum wholesale charges that operators pay for the use of networks in other eu countries. the reduction of roaming charges will take place on 30 april 2016. the maximum level of surcharges will be eur 0,05 per minute for calls, eur 0,02 for sms and eur 0,05 per megabyte of data. these amounts correspond to the ceiling of wholesale tariffs. operators will have to treat all traffic fairly when providing internet access services, in line with the rules on net neutrality. these rules aim to prohibit providers of internet access services from blocking or slowing down content, applications or services of their competitors.
in writing. ‒ the real intentions of this regulation are now even clearer as a result of the negotiations, shattering the illusions of some people during the first reading vote. it is worth recalling the reasons which justified our vote against at first reading. we are facing a giant step forward in the process of deepening the liberalization of the sector, which favours the great powers and their multinationals at the expense of jobs and workers' rights. the attempt to appropriate the internet by the giants of the sector (according to the interests of which this legislative proposal is made) is now being redefined more clearly, and its neutrality is being irrevocably called into question, contrary to what is claimed by the rapporteur and other supporters of this proposal. that alone would justify our vote against it. but there are other reasons for rejecting this proposal, which once again the right wing and the social democrats jointly supported. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of consumers in the event of a breach of the directive. the so-called regulators have been alerted to this, but the european commission has so far not given a satisfactory answer.
in writing. - this report means the abolition of roaming charges in june 2017, the reduction of charges as early as 2016 and open internet access, where operators will be obliged to treat all traffic equally. in a very important conciliation effort by the rapporteur, pilar del castillo, it is ensured that the open market will fulfil its function as a free market without frontiers, where the imposition of a system of roaming charges is not justified.
‒ over the past few months, the european institutions have been in deep negotiations to reach an agreement on the future of the telecommunications market, with the european parliament now in a position to vote on the final agreed package. i therefore vote in favour of this agreement, which aims to introduce harmonised rules to ensure open access to the internet, protect users' rights and end existing surcharges. i would also like to safeguard the fact that the principle of net neutrality is enshrined, thus allowing equal access to information for all without any interference in online traffic. it is also worth mentioning the end of roaming in june 2017, which after so many obstacles and negotiations is thus in a position to end, facilitating communications between citizens or companies.
‒ i voted in favour because i considered it important to abolish roaming as another factor in stimulating the free movement of persons .
in writing. the relaunch of negotiations in the telecommunications sector gained new impetus with the latvian presidency in april this year. however, the mandate given by the council was limited to issues relating to roaming, net neutrality, access and consumer rights, leaving out, for example, the reform of the body of european regulators for electronic communications. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the eu's new rules on the protection of personal data, in particular the rules on the protection of personal data and the rules on the protection of personal data. as regards open access to the internet, i would stress the equal treatment which operators must provide to all consumers of electronic content and applications, preventing them from blocking or restricting services, except in exceptional situations, which i think could have been better specified. in view of the above, i believe that, since regulation is not the ideal, it is always preferable to harmonize the rules of the european electronic communications market rather than a random myriad of disparate national legislation, and i have therefore decided to vote in favour of this report.
‒ the present document is a step forward in the further development of the single market for electronic communications, with a view to its full liberalisation. it favours the great powers and sharpens the interest of multinationals in obtaining a monopoly of electronic communications, which will be done by destroying more jobs and to the detriment of the interest of workers who will be subject to greater pressure to reduce wages and other rights. on the other hand, the principle of neutrality has suffered a significant blow. the commission has also proposed that the maximum number of users should be limited to the number of internet users in the member state concerned. on the other hand, it provides for the controversial zero rating. the possibility of potential abuse of all these exceptions is therefore open.
‒ this document concerns the recommendation for second reading on the council's position at first reading with a view to the adoption of a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending directive 2002/22/ec and regulation (eu) no 531/2012 in the context of the 'single market for electronic communications'. this report aims to deepen the single market for electronic communications in the eu. according to its advocates, electronic communications companies will be able to operate and provide the service wherever their customers are established. however, this is fundamentally a giant step in the further liberalization of the sector which favours the great powers and sharpens the interest of multinationals in obtaining a monopoly in electronic communications. the regulation has positive aspects related to the abolition of roaming charges and net neutrality. the positive aspects do not, however, cancel out a liberalization trend whose consequences will far outweigh them. we voted against it.
‒ regulation (ec) no 1236/2005 is a unique instrument that contributes to the protection of human rights through the control of products and activities that are, or may be, used in an abusive manner to apply the death penalty or to inflict torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, and its revision is an important step towards the objective of further strengthening the eu's role as the main actor in the fight against the death penalty and the eradication of torture. i support the schaake report because i believe that the checklists need to be updated, ensuring an appropriate combination of eu legislative, administrative, judicial and external measures to prevent the production, trade and use of goods intended for torture or products used for lethal, inhuman or degrading purposes. such controls should, however, be proportionate, not create unnecessary burdens restricting trade that has a legitimate purpose, and should take into account judgments of international courts, deliberations of the competent un bodies or reports of the european committee for the prevention of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, etc.
in this report, my vote was naturally against the safeguarding of human rights, the right to life and the right of citizens not to be exposed to cruel or inhuman treatment. the mpt is a humanist party and as such will always be on the side of those who oppose the death penalty and torture. as president of the mpt and as a liberal mep, i voted against the free trade of these substances, which are used for practices that should no longer be allowed in the 21st century.
‒ the anti-torture regulation is a unique instrument that contributes to the protection of human rights by controlling products and activities that are, or may be, used improperly to apply the death penalty or to inflict torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. it also establishes a ban on the trade in 'single-use' products intended for torture and executions and the related technical assistance, as well as a system of authorisation for versatile products which could be misused for torture and executions by lethal injection. i agree that it is important to ensure an appropriate combination of eu legislative, administrative, judicial and external measures in order to prevent and prohibit the production, trade and use of goods intended for torture and to effectively control products that could be used for lethal or inhuman purposes.
in writing. ‒ regulation (ec) no 1236/2005, which aims to combat torture, is an instrument that contributes to the protection of human rights by controlling products and activities that are, or may be, used improperly to apply the death penalty or to inflict torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. it aims to contribute to the objective of eliminating the death penalty worldwide and preventing torture by combining prohibitions with licensing requirements for trade in the listed products. the regulation establishes a ban on trade in 'single-use' products intended for torture and execution, as well as a system of authorisation for versatile products which can be abused to inflict torture and execution by lethal injection. in a context of increasingly complex external trade operations, the effective implementation of controls, checks, sanctions, guidelines and awareness raising actions carried out by national authorities is essential. the rapporteur recalls the need to monitor properly the implementation of member states' commitments, including their obligation to submit and exchange information via a secure and encrypted system on refused authorisations and notifications. we voted in favour.
‒ i voted in favour of the report on trade in certain goods which could be used for capital punishment or for the purpose of torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. it is important that there is a clear and systematic approach to the instrument, combining prohibitions with licensing requirements for trade in certain products. the export control mechanism is and should be in the service of a wider set of objectives, as the rapporteur states.
‒ council regulation (ec) no 1236/2005 establishes controls on trade in certain goods which could be used for capital punishment or for the purpose of torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. the role of the european union in upholding the principle of human dignity needs to be strengthened by revising this regulation and its provisions, thus respecting the basis of european values as laid down in the treaty on european union and the charter of fundamental rights. the proposed amendments relate to the conditions under which transfers of goods, technical assistance and marketing are carried out. in the field of external trade operations, member states should strengthen the capacity to suspend or prohibit the transfer of products that are used for lethal or inhumane purposes. legislative conditions should be created to provide for an effective regulation of this type of trade. i am voting in favour of the proposal as it seeks to strengthen protection against human rights violations and to ensure balanced and controlled conditions for international trade, while respecting the legitimate interests of companies and the possible use of these products.
‒ i consider it crucial to prohibit trade in goods that could be used to apply the death penalty or to inflict torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. i voted in favour of the text because i consider it fair and balanced.
‒ i support this report, which seeks to amend regulation (ec) no 1236/2005 on trade in certain goods which could be used for capital punishment, torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. the european parliament has stressed in the last five years of the regulation that it would be necessary to adapt it to the current reality, given the strong evidence of the use of medicines exported from the eu for the use of the death penalty in third countries. as such, i welcome the amendment of annexes ii and iii to the regulation, concerning the lists of prohibited and regulated goods, as well as the revision of the regulation itself, highlighting as positive aspects the control of exports used for illicit purposes, the prohibition on the provision of brokering services relating to goods the marketing of which involves the use of the death penalty, torture or other cruel treatment and the exchange of information between customs authorities. although we are faced with amendments which are not consensual and which involve opposition from the business community, which calls for legitimate trade, i think it is essential to strike a careful balance between this business interest and the full guarantee of effective control of the use of certain products for illegitimate purposes.
‒ the revision of this regulation to make the export of goods liable to be used for capital punishment or for the purpose of torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment a necessary evolution of the existing legislative framework. it seeks, however, without creating excessive bureaucratic barriers, which could make it difficult to export goods which can be used for various purposes, a balanced solution. it therefore focuses the prohibition on the purpose of the goods, thereby ensuring their use in accordance with the protection of human rights. it is a path that calls for and involves european businesses and their partners across borders in a commitment to defend human rights. it carries a fundamental ethical dimension: liability for transactions in this type of goods does not end when the goods are delivered, but continues until they are used. this regulation also demonstrated that the european union is taking its role as a defender of human rights beyond its borders. it is therefore a further step in strengthening the eu's role as the main responsible actor worldwide in the fight against the death penalty and the eradication of torture.
in the first place, the commission has to be able to take account of the fact that the european parliament has already adopted a resolution on the situation in the former yugoslavia. this proposal for a regulation deserves the clear political support of the european parliament, in particular the idea of creating a union general export authorisation for countries with firm international commitments and the introduction of an urgent procedure to allow for a rapid update of the control lists. the report also improves the system by extending the number of products controlled, allowing trade in goods, including those not explicitly listed in the regulation, to be stopped by customs authorities if there are reasonable grounds to believe that the products will be used to apply the death penalty, inflict torture or other ill-treatment. i therefore supported this contribution from the european parliament because it makes eu trade policy more consistent with europe's commitment to human rights and ensures that european companies are not complicit in inhumane practices.
‒ regulation no 1236/2005, which aims to combat torture, is an instrument that contributes to the protection of human rights by controlling products and activities that are, or may be, used improperly to apply the death penalty or to inflict torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. it aims to contribute to the objective of eliminating the death penalty and preventing torture by combining prohibitions with licensing requirements for trade in the listed products. the regulation establishes a prohibition on trade in 'single-use' products intended for torture and executions and related technical assistance and a system of authorisation for versatile products that could be misused for torture and executions by lethal injection. in a context of increasingly complex external trade operations, the effective implementation of controls, checks, sanctions, guidelines and awareness raising actions carried out by national authorities is essential. the rapporteur recalls the need to monitor properly the implementation of member states' commitments, including their obligation to submit and exchange information via a secure and encrypted system on refused authorisations and notifications. we voted in favour.
in writing. the proposal, which obliges member states to exchange automatically information on crossborder tax rulings, is part of a series of initiatives aimed at preventing tax avoidance by companies. the new rules should apply from 1 january 2017. the truth is that member states share very little information with each other about their tax agreements, leaving it to their discretion to decide whether a tax agreement may be relevant to another eu country. the lack of transparency on tax agreements is exploited by certain companies to artificially reduce their tax contribution. however, it could have gone further, in particular by increasing transparency. the directive requires member states to exchange automatically information on 'cross-border' tax rulings, leaving out purely national rulings.
‒ the aim of amending directive 2011/16/eu is to make it applicable to the automatic exchange of information in the field of taxation. in this connection, it is intended to establish administrative cooperation between the tax authorities (ta) of the member states as regards the mandatory automatic exchange of information on advance crossborder tax and transfer pricing arrangements. the proposal also provides that member states receiving information may request additional information in greater detail. it should be noted that prior agreements between the ta and companies such as those at the root of the well-known scandal in luxembourg (luxleaks), in which the current president of the european commission was directly involved are a widespread practice, along with the phenomena of base erosion and profit shifting. this proposal may put some grains in a wheel that deprives sovereign states and their people of the vast millions of euros of resources owed to them by multinationals when paying taxes on profits. resources that are drained from the workers and their families through an unbearable tax burden. the commission has not yet addressed such pressing issues as tax havens, which are veritable sinks of public funds, veritable havens of crime and money laundering.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the proposal to oblige member states to exchange automatically information on crossborder tax rulings in order to prevent tax evasion by companies. this is a very important proposal for a directive, when it is estimated that corporate tax avoidance deprives the public budgets of eu member states of several billion euros a year.
‒ the european parliament stressed in its resolution of 21 may 2013 that the european union should take a leading role in the global debate on the fight against tax fraud, tax evasion and tax havens, especially as regards the promotion of the exchange of information. currently, with directive 2011/16/eu on administrative cooperation in force, member states share very little information with each other about their tax arrangements. the proposed amendment, as amended by directive 2014/107/eu, introduces a new article in the directive, which defines the scope and conditions for the mandatory automatic exchange of information on cross-border tax and transfer pricing arrangements. this obligation is extended to agreements concluded in the 10 years preceding the date on which the proposed directive takes effect and which are still valid on the date of entry into force of the directive. i believe that this commission proposal will be an important step towards increasing tax transparency and continuing the fight against crossborder tax evasion.
‒ i voted in favour, as i believe that there is a need to increase transparency and the exchange of information in tax matters in order to avoid, among other consequences, distortion of competition.
‒ the challenge posed by crossborder tax avoidance, aggressive tax planning and harmful tax competition has increased considerably and is a matter of concern to governments at european and global level. the european parliament has always stressed the need for the eu to take a leading position against fraud, tax evasion and tax havens and, in doing so, attaches particular importance to enhanced administrative cooperation and transparency in cross-border tax agreements, which allow for the exchange of information between member states, avoiding potential negative effects on their tax bases and reducing the impact of tax evasion. i am in favour of the adoption of this report on a special legislative consultation procedure concerning the proposal for a council directive amending directive 2011/16/eu as regards the mandatory automatic exchange of information in the field of taxation. i would like to highlight as a positive aspect the introduction of a new article on the scope and conditions for the mandatory automatic exchange of information on crossborder tax and transfer pricing agreements between member states, and highlight as a negative point the missed opportunity to include purely national and prior transfer pricing agreements in this framework.
in writing. ‒ it is important to be able to provide for the best way to share information effectively between tax authorities and to help reinforce good tax behaviour by large companies. tax evasion causes considerable losses, which inevitably affect national budgets and result in an overburden of taxes on other economic operators and, in particular, on workers. this text helps to prevent budgetary losses resulting from tax abuse by large companies and thus to encourage a greater margin of comfort for national budgets, which are already under pressure.
‒ in the wake of the offshoreleaks, luxleaks and swissleak tax scandals, the european institutions appear to be engaged in this battle against tax fraud and evasion. however, we must ensure that all the measures and proposals under way are not just a piece of legislation, keeping everything the same. or let 's see: the council's proposal on the automatic exchange of information represents a clear setback from initial expectations; the regulation on the exchange of information with switzerland contains several subterfuge to its compliance; the work of the taxe committee has always been difficult. thirteen governments, including those of the netherlands, luxembourg and the united kingdom, have refused access to the documents of the code of conduct group; the reservations about making public the tax agreements and country declarations of multinationals are evident. these are signs that make us doubt the real political will to tackle the problem. indeed, the further we go, the clearer the commitment of the leading figures and parties supporting the eu institutions, starting with the presidents of the european commission and the eurogroup.
in writing. ‒ the aim of amending directive 2011/16/eu is to make it provide for the automatic exchange of information in the field of taxation. in this regard, it is intended to establish administrative cooperation between the tax authorities of the member states as regards the mandatory automatic exchange of information on advance cross-border tax rulings and advance transfer pricing arrangements. we do not agree with the justification that the necessity of mandatory automatic exchange is essentially justified in order to promote the proper functioning of the single market. we nevertheless regarded the objective as positive and therefore voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ this resolution addresses and defends many of the principles i have been advocating in the context of the european union's foreign policy. as the world's leading actor in development and humanitarian aid, it has a special responsibility to promote the right to universal access to health care, and is required to be one step ahead of all other actors. i think it is extremely important that the european union should try to act on two fronts in this context: on the one hand, in terms of development aid, which includes essential investments in the field of health, and on the other hand, in terms of the indispensable assistance for the economic recovery of the countries most affected by the ebola epidemic. i shall vote in favour of this and other aspects of the text and hope that it will be adopted.
in writing. ‒ since march 2014, sierra leone, liberia and guinea have been hit by the most severe ebola outbreak known to date. at the local, regional, national and global levels, the ebola crisis is systemic. however, the international community has been slow to understand the gravity of the situation and to react, with ngos being more effective, better informed and better placed to be on the frontline in the fight against ebola. i support this report because i believe it is essential that, on the basis of this experience, we should start preparing for the post-ebola period now. the european union must act on two fronts: on the one hand, in terms of development aid, which includes essential investments in the field of health, and on the other hand, in terms of the indispensable assistance for the economic recovery of the three countries. the european development fund (edf) programme for these three countries should be reassessed in the light of the multiple challenges created by the ebola crisis. i welcome the eu's willingness to devote at least 20% of public aid to the development of basic social sectors, giving priority to health.
in writing. ‒ since march 2014, sierra leone, liberia and guinea have been victims of the worst ebola outbreak in human history. the permeability of borders has facilitated the passage of the virus from one country to another. the three countries concerned are among the lowest in the undp human development index. its average life expectancy is less than 60 years, schooling rarely exceeds three years and about 80% of its citizens live in extreme poverty. it is therefore clear that these three countries cannot solve the problem on their own. the european parliament remains true to its tradition and recalls that its task is to control the executive, to exercise its prerogatives as legislator and to give political impetus. the european union must therefore respond to the challenges ahead in the fight against ebola. i agree that the current ebola crisis reveals the structural gaps that still exist in many countries and, on the other hand, reminds european union leaders of the need to persevere in their desire to devote at least 20% of public aid to the development of basic social sectors, giving priority to health.
in writing. this report looks at the ebola crisis in liberia, sierra leone and guinea-conacri and seeks to draw lessons from it. the report is contradictory, including some clearly positive aspects, others not so much, and also some negative aspects. it is important that for the first time the disastrous effects of the imf and world bank interventions on the deterioration of the health and education systems in these and other more vulnerable countries are recognised. positive recommendations are made on the increase in development aid by the eu and its member states, the need to reorient the priorities of the european development fund to match the real priorities of these countries (public services, especially health, support for small-scale production, family farming, etc.) and access to medicines, pointing out the problem of 'patent dictatorship'. but the report is not always consistent in advocating universal and free access to health services. while some paragraphs make this requirement explicit, others use more ambiguous terms such as 'comprehensive services'. the public-private partnership model advocated for medicines, on the other hand, overrides the desirable preponderance of strong public capacity in this area. in acknowledging the efforts of countries and organizations to combat the epidemic, an essential reference to cuba is missing.
‒ there is still little knowledge about the transmission and mutation potential of the ebola virus. the european union's commitment to contain the spread of the ebola virus and its support for the development of logistics and research to respond to the crisis should be recalled, but the lessons we have learned from the need to strengthen health systems in developing countries should not be forgotten. these types of epidemics require transnational cooperation for outbreak assessment and management.
‒ the ebola virus has created an international public health emergency with countries such as sierra leone, liberia and guinea suffering the worst ebola outbreak in human history. the scale of this catastrophe is due to political, cross-border, surveillance, diagnosis, research, and other factors. the european union must play a leading role in this matter, helping to advance a coherent national health system for each of these countries. the development of health systems worldwide, with a particular focus on developing countries, should involve new investments in infrastructure, surveillance and information systems, the supply of medicines, human resources and the management of health services themselves. the role of ngos is central and it is of the utmost importance to further develop their skills in the future. i support this report, stressing the need to develop local health systems with the support of the european union and to implement effective information and communication conditions as a means of prevention.
‒ the ebola crisis has shown that, despite some initial delays in the international response, there has been a strong response from the european union and its member states to combat the spread of the virus, as well as a strong commitment in the areas of humanitarian and development aid. in fact, this serious crisis has turned out to be a real test for the international community, as ebola has proved to be a systemic epidemic capable of taking on a transnational dimension. for this reason, the contingency plans called for consistent and responsible international cooperation, bringing together efforts in the areas of research, innovation and crisis management, but also long-term investments in strengthening health systems and governance, particularly in terms of public health, in developing countries. i therefore support the urgent need for these countries to invest in the health sector, equipping it with specialists in the various fields as well as logistical facilities, which can ensure quality medical care, and, in parallel, the importance of reviewing the programming of the 11th european development fund, with a view to ensuring that investments in health and good governance become priority areas for all countries with public infrastructures considered to be fragile.
‒ i voted in favour of the report on the ebola crisis because the european parliament makes very important recommendations to strengthen health systems in developing countries and prevent future epidemics (ebola and other diseases). the report recalls that the current outbreak in west africa reveals the serious gaps in many countries in all essential services and calls for the appropriate lessons to be drawn from this crisis. the report recommends and insists on the following: strengthening eu aid to developing countries in the field of health and other basic social sectors (education and training, sanitation, food security and clean water); eu assistance to the economic recovery of the three countries most affected by ebola (sierra leone, liberia and guinea); the creation of a permanent european rapid reaction team; and finally the creation of a network of monitoring points in developing countries to detect, as early as possible, new cases of infectious diseases that could become pandemics. the report is an important contribution to future union responses in terms of prevention and management of health crises and therefore deserves my vote in favour.
‒ we must recognize that the imf and world bank programmes have devastated the fragile health infrastructure in these countries, devastated public health services, and more, creating a situation of inability to cope with the progression of the epidemic. it is therefore essential to reverse this process and support the construction of universal, free public health systems; the training of specialised health personnel. we must combat the hegemony of pharmaceutical companies in the development of new medicines, the dictatorship of patents; we must support the development of essential public services, such as water and sanitation; we must cancel the external debt of these countries. we welcome, however, and we are grateful for all the international aid that is still needed, and it is worth recalling here the giant example of a small country - cuba - which alone has sent more doctors and nurses to the affected countries than all the other western countries combined.
‒ this report analyses the ebola crisis in liberia, sierra leone and guinea. the rapporteur considers that the scale of the disaster can be attributed to a number of factors: the political inability of the affected countries to raise the alarm, the inadequate response of the international community, the devastating effects of the closure of borders and the restrictions imposed on people, the ineffectiveness of the surveillance and alert mechanisms, the slow and poorly adapted response when aid was mobilised, the glaring lack of leadership by the who and the lack of research and development in the field of medicines, diagnostics and vaccines. the report's most negative aspects include its uncritical tone towards the slow international response, particularly that of the eu, and its call for the european commission to launch a broad public-private partnership to 'strengthen national health systems and facilitate transfers of results to the population', an approach that is contrary to the objectives it seeks to achieve. we abstained.
in writing. ‒ on 18 september 2015, the united states environmental protection agency (epa) and the california air resources board (carb) issued a warning of pollution violations by diesel vehicles of the volkswagen group, and the group later admitted to having installed software that detected when the car was being tested, reducing the amount of emissions. i support this resolution in which the european parliament condemns all fraud perpetrated by car manufacturers and calls on the companies to assume all their responsibilities and to cooperate with the authorities in the investigations. the european commission should rethink the current type-approval system to ensure that type-approvals and certificates from the competent national authorities can be independently verified. the european commission and the competent authorities of all member states should have the right to re-evaluate the type-approval and certificate of conformity, and to require the withdrawal and the end of the placing on the market of vehicles, when they have evidence of non-compliance with eu emission limit values. the commission should adopt and apply the new real driving emissions test cycle without delay.
the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' in the context of the directive. it is recalled that air pollution causes more than 430 000 premature deaths in the eu each year and has an estimated cost of eur 940 billion due to its health effects. the automotive industry is a major driver of growth and innovation, contributing to employment in a significant number of member states, and in the absence of firm action, the current scandal could jeopardise the reputation and competitiveness of the entire sector, as it has affected millions of deceived and misled consumers. i condemn any fraud perpetrated by car manufacturers, and companies must take full responsibility for their actions and cooperate fully with the authorities in their investigations. it is essential that the commission and the member states quickly restore consumer confidence through concrete measures and make every possible effort to defuse the situation.

the rapporteur. madam president, the court of justice of the european union launched a legislative initiative in 2011 to amend its statute to allow the appointment of 12 additional judges to the general court. in april 2014, this claim was approved by parliament at first reading. however, the council never appointed any of these 12 judges because the member states could not reach an agreement on the choice of judges, as each state wanted to appoint its own judge and the number of judges to be appointed, 12, did not coincide with the number of nominating states, 28. thus, in october 2014, the court came to ask for 28 more judges, double the existing ones, as well as the abolition of the court of the civil service. in april 2014, 12 more judges were needed to resolve the alleged problems of the court, but by october of that same year, 28 more judges were needed, as well as the extinction of one court. it is obvious that this is not a question of solving any court problem, but of solving a problem of the council, which is not able to appoint members who do not coincide with its members. the proposal under discussion is not merely an amendment to the original legislative proposal, but a new proposal, since it is no longer just the appointment of 12 more judges, but 28 more and the abolition of a specialised court, as provided for in the treaties of nice and lisbon. the commission, however, was obliged to give its opinion on the content of the new legislative proposal, which it did not do, since it only gave its opinion on the appointment of 12 more judges and not 28 more, and it never gave any opinion on the abolition of the civil service tribunal. the treaty provides for the creation of specialised courts, not their abolition. the abolition of the civil service tribunal would mean abandoning the system of specialised courts provided for in the treaties of nice and lisbon, when it is generally recognised that specialised justice is a better quality of justice and therefore the possibility of creating new specialised courts, in particular for trademarks and patents, should be considered instead of trying to abolish the only one that exists, and whose success is recognised by all. such a reform should be preceded by an impact study, which would clarify for the co-legislators - council and parliament - its need, its scope, its costs and other consequences. however, this study was never carried out. in the light of the irrationality of the council's proposal, i proposed in my report to reconstitute the position adopted by parliament at its first reading in april 2014 as the increase from 12 judges to 28 judges will not be well understood by european public opinion, as it would result in an increase in the union's structural expenditure of more than eur 20 million per year, simply because the council was not able to appoint the approved judges. at a time when many countries are undergoing strict austerity measures and the european union is proposing to reduce staff and cut public expenditure, increasing the union's structural public expenditure would set a bad example for the whole of europe. but the council was not amenable to this position and has maintained its position, and it is now up to parliament to accept or reject this claim on behalf of the european taxpayers whom we represent. in my report i also proposed absolute respect for gender parity in the recruitment of judges, but this rule was also rejected by the council on the grounds that the treaties do not allow its adoption, replacing it with a mere statement in the recitals, without any legal value. if the council's position is accepted by parliament, then we will have to assume that in the european union, effective gender equality is nothing more than a rhetorical proclamation, without normative content or binding legal force. we must therefore assume that the constitutional law of the union does not allow the realisation of a fundamental right which is, moreover, one of the founding values of the european union itself. that is why i also ask for the council's position to be rejected and for parliament to be returned to its first reading.

in writing. ‒ a reform of the court of justice of the european union is urgently needed because of the over-working of the court. the court pointed to the need for 12 judges in addition to the 28 it already has, one per member state. however, the member states in the council could not agree on which countries would be entitled to an additional judge. they decided to double the number of judges (up to 56), a number clearly higher than that proposed by the court itself, which represents a colossal and unnecessary expense for the european public purse. i voted in favour of an increase in line with what had been recommended by the real needs of the court's functioning - up to 40 judges - noting the justified increase in the number of judges and avoiding a useless and megalomaniacal decision. the european union must take decisions, not in accordance with national egocentricities which prevent an efficient decision, but in accordance with the real administrative needs of the union.
‒ this report constitutes a second reading of the proposal for a regulation on the reform of the statute of the court of justice. the council proposed two changes to the organisation of the general court: (1) that the number of judges at the general court should be fixed at 56 at the end of a three-stage procedure; (2) that the civil service tribunal, which has jurisdiction to rule at first instance in proceedings concerning the european union civil service, should be closed and the judges transferred to the general court. parliament did not reject the council's proposals outright, but merely amended the proposed timetable for increasing the number of judges by introducing more steps and adding the need for gender balance in the appointment of judges. for our part, we do not agree with the proposal. we are against the closure of the civil service tribunal, since under article 270 tfeu the tribunal has jurisdiction to hear disputes between the eu and the approximately 35 000 civil servants. we also believe that simply increasing the number of judges will not solve the problem of the overload of cases facing the general court, beyond the disagreement over the proposed method of selection.

‒ established in 1949, the general fisheries commission for the mediterranean (gfcm) provides an appropriate framework for multilateral cooperation in order to promote the development, conservation, rational management and better use of living marine resources in the mediterranean and the black sea at levels considered sustainable and with a low risk of rupture. at its annual sessions in 2011, 2012 and 2013, the gfcm adopted a set of recommendations with a view to the sustainable exploitation of red coral, the reduction of incidental catches of seabirds, sea turtles and cetaceans, the conservation of monk seals, sharks and rays in the gfcm agreement area, and the sustainable development of small pelagic stocks in the adriatic sea. following the adoption of parliament's position at first reading, informal negotiations were opened on 13 january 2015 with a view to swiftly reaching an agreement at second reading on the incorporation of those measures into regulation (eu) no 1343/2011. after two rounds of trilogue, an agreement was reached between parliament and the council, and now, following the recommendation of the pech committee, the council's position at first reading must be adopted without amendment. i voted in favour.

‒ the union rules on novel foods were established by regulation (ec) no 258/97 of the european parliament and of the council and commission regulation (ec) no 1852/2001, which recognises that any novel food or food ingredient requires a prior authorisation before it can be placed on the market in order to preserve a high level of protection of human health and consumer interests. in the light of rapid scientific and technological progress in the food sector, there is a range of novel foods and food ingredients, such as foods containing, consisting of or produced from micro-organisms, fungi and algae, or foods with an intentionally modified primary molecular structure, which do not fall within the scope of the definition of 'novel food' in the current legislation. i am voting in favour of this report which seeks to fill this gap and adapt the definition of novel foods to these realities while reducing the administrative burden on applicants by simplifying and rationalising the regulatory authorisation process.

‒ the rules on so-called novel foods (i.e. foods which were not used in a significant way for human consumption in the eu before may 1997) are currently set out in regulation (ec) no 258/97 and regulation (ec) no 1852/2001. in view of the scientific and technological progress since the entry into force of these regulations, the commission submitted in december 2013 a proposal to review and adapt the existing regulation, which was approved with amendments by envi in november 2014. following interinstitutional negotiations between december 2014 and june 2015, an agreement has been reached. in line with the commitment reached, the new rules aim to address the main concerns raised in the broad consultation of industry, namely: clarification of the definition of novel food; subjecting novel foods to a harmonised assessment and authorisation process; simplification and rationalisation of the authorisation process; and providing for a robust data protection regime. the new legislation also transitionally regulates the placing on the market of food derived from cloned animals and defines what nanomaterials are. i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ regulation (ec) no 258/97 of the european parliament and of the council and commission regulation (ec) no 1852/2001 are the legislative instruments establishing the union rules on novel foods. it is commonly accepted by consumers, food business operators and policy-makers that any novel food or food ingredient requires prior authorisation before it is placed on the market in order to preserve a high level of protection of human health, its traceability and, of course, the interests of consumers. however, scientific and technological progress in the food sector has shown the need to revise the definition of 'novel food' in regulation (ec) no 258/97 to include, inter alia, novel foods produced from micro-organisms, fungi and algae. i therefore support the report by mr james nicholson on the proposal for a european parliament and council decision to close this gap by adapting the definition to new foods on the market and at the same time reducing unnecessary administrative burdens in the regulatory authorisation process, in order to promote innovation and the competitiveness of the european food sector.

‒ this legislative proposal sets new national emission limit values for certain air pollutants with the aim of reducing threats to human health, the environment and the climate. poor air quality contributes to premature death, sickness absence from work, significant health costs, lost productivity, lost crop yields and damage to buildings. in europe, the total external costs to society related to health and caused by air pollution are estimated at between eur 330 and 940 billion per year. according to the report, member states should at least limit their emissions of sulphur dioxide (so2), nitrogen oxides (nox), non-methane volatile organic compounds (nmvoc), ammonia (nh3), particulate matter (pm2,5) and mercury (hg). the containment of non-methane volatile organic compounds (nmvocs) and methane (ch4) should be placed in the broader context of reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
‒ for pressing environmental and public health reasons, air quality concerns everyone. it is by its nature a cross-border issue which demands immediate action after years of political neglect. the proposal revises the 2001 directive on national emission limit values for certain air pollutants. it's part of the clean air package. it is proposed to amend the emission limits for air pollutants, in particular sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, ammonia and non-methane volatile organic compounds, for 2020 and 2030. mercury has also been added to this list, with limits for this element to be introduced only from 2020. in addition, the scope of the directive is extended to include particulate matter (pm2,5) from 2020 and, with a view to convergence with climate legislation, methane from 2030. the new 2030 targets in the proposal are the most complex element, with different limits for each member state and each pollutant, based on achieving 70% of the maximum technically feasible reductions in health impacts as defined by the who. we have supported this report, although there are some contradictory elements. we reiterate that the regulatory approach must prevail over market approaches.

‒ eusair is the eu's third macro-regional strategy and is well placed to draw on the lessons and experiences of the eu strategy for the baltic sea region and the eu strategy for the danube region. this strategy builds on existing cooperation in the region, notably the adriatic-ionian initiative and the adriatic-ionian euroregion, whose members are 26 regional and local authorities from seven countries. eusair covers eight countries equally represented by eu member states (croatia, greece, italy and slovenia) and third countries, all of them with the status of candidate countries (albania, montenegro and serbia) or potential candidates (bosnia and herzegovina). the region has over 70 million inhabitants and plays a key role in strengthening geographical continuity in europe. eusair is a unique opportunity for the countries of the region to turn over a new leaf and put economic and political problems behind them, working together, guided by the commission, towards prosperity and sustainable development.

‒ cohesion policy represents more than one third of the eu budget and is its main investment instrument. therefore, since the 2014-2020 cohesion policy is fully aligned with and contributes to the achievement of the objectives of the strategy, it is very important to examine the progress already made, the scope of the review and the challenges that need to be addressed from the perspective of cohesion policy. the europe 20-20 strategy is a comprehensive long-term strategy for 'growth and jobs' built around five objectives: employment, innovation, climate change and energy sustainability, education and the fight against poverty and social exclusion. the review of this strategy, which will precede the submission of the proposal for the mid-term review of the multiannual financial framework 2014-2020, will provide the basis for the future architecture of cohesion policy after 2020.
‒ the report is quite clear on several points as to what it seeks to achieve: reconciling cohesion policies under the 2014-2020 multiannual financial framework with the objectives of the eu 2020 strategy - understood as being in line with eu cohesion. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover all the activities of the european union. in other words, it defends one of the worst aspects of the current cohesion policy its submission to a neoliberal agenda of withdrawal of rights and weakening of the state and its social functions, privatisations, which is the eu2020 strategy. that is, submission to an agenda which is itself a generator of divergence rather than cohesion. the eu2020 objectives, which are markedly lagging behind, for example in the social field, have a federalist framework and an artificial and bureaucratic definition, leading to a decrease in cohesion in the sociological and territorial context. the combination of cohesion policies, the european structural investment funds and the multiannual financial framework is making these more dependent on the eu's macro objectives and not on the specific development needs of the member states. obviously, we can only vote against.
‒ i welcome the adoption of the report on cohesion policy and the review of the europe 2020 strategy. i congratulate the rapporteur on the work he has done in an area which represents more than a third of the european union budget. cohesion policy, by covering all regions, is one of the most important instruments for promoting growth and competitiveness, reducing disparities and asymmetries between regions.
‒ cohesion policy for 2014-2020 is the eu's main investment and development policy, aligned with the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy for smart, sustainable and inclusive growth. it aims to reduce disparities between regions and promote convergence, with a budget of €351.8 billion by the end of 2020 i therefore vote in favour of this mid-term review report on the europe 2020 strategy, which calls for better linkage between the five objectives of the strategy - employment, innovation, climate change and energy sustainability, education and the fight against poverty and social exclusion - and its flagship initiatives. i believe that the revision of cohesion policy must give new impetus to the outermost regions which suffer from natural economic and social constraints as explained in article 349 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union.
in writing. it was with great satisfaction that i saw my own-initiative report on 'cohesion policy and the revision of the europe 2020 strategy' approved by the european parliament by more than 80% of the votes cast (530 votes in favour, 75 against and 54 abstentions). the importance of this report goes far beyond the political issues dealt with by the committee on regional development, as it is the first document with the european parliament's backing on the review of the europe 2020 strategy, and it also launches the interinstitutional debate on this subject (which starts with the commission at this plenary session) as well as the discussion on the mid-term review of the multiannual financial framework (mff). as 2019 is a year of european political events and coincides with the end of the current mff and the current europe 2020 strategy, we hope that the discussions we are now starting will also take into account a broader time horizon and, in particular, the future european legislative framework after 2020. i wanted to make a comprehensive document that was nonetheless positive and easy to read. thanks to the positive and cooperative attitude of the shadow rapporteurs and of the colleagues who have amended the document, i believe that i have achieved the objectives i set out to achieve.
‒ as a result of the economic and financial crisis in some member states, the funds which give substance to cohesion policy and which are intended to finance projects aimed at promoting it have become of crucial importance. they have guaranteed investment capacity for the economic recovery of countries with macroeconomic imbalances. the economic governance recommendations should take this into account and ensure that the regions are safeguarded as recipients of these funds. in this europe 2020 mid-term review, the uneven impact of the crisis must be taken into account. different territorial and social characteristics have led to different resilience capacities. look at youth unemployment in the outermost regions. multi-level governance mechanisms should recognise the capacity of regional and local authorities to intervene. i would like to conclude with a warning: although the operational programmes have been agreed, their implementation is still in its infancy, which has created difficulties.
in writing. ‒ we agree with the strategic objectives of cohesion policy. we cannot understand why the poorer countries and regions differ from the european average. this is the case in portugal, which, since the euro came into operation, has consistently diverged from the european union average in terms of gdp per capita. so something is wrong. there is no cohesion. policies are not working. because the macroeconomic framework is not consistent with regional development policies. in other words, austerity policies, the containment of public spending, whether good or bad, do not allow the establishment of virtuous dynamics of local or regional development. i can give you examples of projects that are not going to work because there is no funding. because the bank prefers to speculate. we can see funds that are not being used in portugal because of the impositions of the troika and the necessary adjustment aimed at the so-called consolidation of public finances. the result is in sight. after almost thirty years of integration, portugal is poorer, more dependent and has the highest public debt in its history.
‒ the report makes clear, in several points, what it wants: the reconciliation of cohesion policies, under the 2014-2020 financial framework, with the achievement of the europe 2020 objectives - understood as being in line with cohesion in the eu. it thus aims to create ex ante conditionalities and link the country specific recommendations to the programming of the funds for 2014-2020. while, on the one hand, from a union perspective, it is rational to reconcile the various investments, avoiding overlaps and contradictions, on the other hand, the definition of the europe 2020 objectives has a federalist framework and an artificial and bureaucratic definition, leading to a decrease in cohesion in the sociological and territorial context. the combination of the european structural investment funds and the multiannual financial framework with cohesion policies is making them dependent on the eu's macro objectives and not on the specific development needs of the member states. we voted against it.
‒ the european parliament's co-rapporteurs for the common provisions regulation proposed the deletion of all macroeconomic conditionality provisions. several amendments were tabled, for example, on behalf of various political groups in parliament which also proposed the abolition of these provisions. however, macroeconomic conditionality was eventually incorporated into the regulation. the agreement reached by parliament, the council and the commission was approved without the amendments seeking to abolish it having been put to the vote. this own-initiative report does not permit the deletion or amendment of the provisions of article 23 of the cpr as contained in the regulation. it can only ensure that those provisions are applied in the most justified and balanced way possible. i voted yes.
‒ the report proposes to reconcile the esi funds and other eu cohesion instruments with what it calls 'good economic governance', under the framework of the european semester and its entire arsenal of conditions for the activity of states and their macroeconomic policies, with country-specific recommendations, reform plans, etc., without forgetting the very 'macroeconomic conditionality' in the regulation on the funds, which provides that payments and commitments of investment funds are suspended in the event of 'non-compliance'. the report contains positive aspects, such as criticism of the suspension of funding (which, however, admits that it should be applied in exceptional cases and reveal greater 'flexibility') and the recognition that the mechanisms associated with the european semester affect the operability and implementation of the esi funds and that the implementation of the mechanisms should not affect the policy objectives and targets of the esi funds. in a sense, you want to square the circle. but the overall objective of the report is to ensure that the european semester mechanisms have a territorial and integrated dimension, and also to ensure that they are more 'democratic' (through control by the european parliament), more flexible and tolerant in the face of member states' failure to comply. in other words, in practice the report accepts and seeks to legitimize the unacceptable and the illegitimate. we voted against it.
‒ i share the view that the existence of a stable macroeconomic environment is conducive to the correct and successful implementation of the european structural and investment funds. the reprogramming process can be costly and difficult for national, local and regional administrations to manage, so the procedure under article 23 of the regulation should be used in exceptional cases, avoiding the creation of financial instability and uncertainty. i voted in favour of the report presented, regretting that the european parliament does not have a more active role in monitoring the application of the mechanism of that article.
‒ in the previous round of cohesion policy negotiations, the various groups in the european parliament expressed their reservations about the introduction of macroeconomic conditionality, which allows for a suspension of payments from the structural funds when a member state is in breach of european economic rules. however, macroeconomic conditionality was eventually introduced into the cohesion policy funds regulation and several changes to the initial way of operation were adopted. i therefore vote in favour of this report which allows for a greater interlinking between the funds and economic governance, while ensuring that the achievement of the political objectives and targets of the european funds should not be jeopardised by the mechanisms of economic governance.
in the case of the commission, the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on the protection of personal data are respected. the text adopted aims to clarify a number of elements concerning the application of the first part of article 23 of the regulation on common provisions (on the practical implications of the reprogramming and suspension of the european structural and investment funds - esi funds), adopted in the previous mandate. the rapporteur therefore calls for the rules to be applied 'in the most justified and balanced way possible' and for the provisions of this article to be used only as a 'last resort' and only to make the esi funds more efficient and effective. the committee also calls for greater involvement not only of local and regional authorities in the reprogramming exercise but also of the european parliament in the scrutiny of the whole governance system provided for in article 23. because i consider that the rapporteur has put to the vote a well-considered text which expresses a comprehensive position of the european parliament, i have voted in favour of this motion for a resolution.
‒ the structural funds are a key instrument for promoting territorial and economic cohesion and for boosting the economy of countries with macroeconomic imbalances. the economic governance recommendations in these cases must take this into account and ensure that the regions are safeguarded as recipients of these funds.
‒ the report proposes a reconciliation between the strategic investment funds (sifs) and other eu cohesion instruments with the european semester framework, macroeconomic policies and the specific recommendations for member states, specifically with reference to article 23 of the cpr (which advocates that payments and commitments of investment funds be suspended in case of non-compliance). the report contains positive points, such as the criticism of the suspension of funding in reference to article 23 of the cpr. recognises that the mechanisms associated with the european semester affect the operability of cohesion policy and in particular the implementation of the structural funds. this report is therefore unacceptable in that it ends up legitimising an instrument which should be banned from the eu.
in writing. the report proposes a reconciliation between the esi funds and other eu cohesion instruments with the european semester framework, macroeconomic policies and the specific recommendations to member states, specifically with reference to article 23 of the cpr (which calls for the suspension of payments and commitments of investment funds in case of non-compliance). the report argues that this suspension should be applied in exceptional cases and should be more flexible. further recognises that the mechanisms associated with the european semester affect the operability and implementation of the esi funds. however, the overall objective of the report is to ensure that the european semester mechanisms have a territorial and integrated dimension, creating the illusion that their democratic nature is possible (especially through control by the european parliament). the aim is to legitimize the eu's governance policies by giving it a more democratic and development-oriented outfit, recognising that their implementation has been harmful. we voted against it.
